messages.content: I want to design a distributed scheduler that preserves tenant quota ownership and performance isolation during tenant migration, adversarial workloads, and network partitions. Quota ownership must never duplicate during migration, crashes, or partitions, and disconnected schedulers must not exceed their assigned quotas. On healthy workers, unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency must remain within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline.

The design has two requirements that must hold together. The quota rule is a safety invariant: migration, a crash, or a partition must never leave the same quota owned in two places, and a disconnected scheduler must stay within the quota assigned to it. The isolation rule concerns latency: on healthy workers, each unaffected tenant’s p99 dispatch latency must be no more than twice that tenant’s workload-matched isolated baseline. Meeting one rule would not establish that the other is met.
When you say quota ownership must never duplicate, does that include a brief overlap during a tenant migration?

Yes. “Never” includes the handoff itself. A migration cannot temporarily make the same tenant quota available to both the departing and receiving sides. The requirement is stronger than saying that any overlap will eventually be corrected.
What if the migration is interrupted by a crash or a network partition?

The ownership rule still applies. Neither an interrupted handoff nor uncertainty about another scheduler’s state permits a second copy of the quota to be treated as owned. The design has to preserve nonduplicated ownership across migration, crashes, and partitions, including when those circumstances coincide.
Can a disconnected scheduler continue dispatching work?

The stated rule does not categorically forbid it. It does forbid a disconnected scheduler from exceeding its assigned quota, and continued dispatch cannot rely on duplicating quota ownership elsewhere. Whether it can dispatch in a particular situation depends on what quota it can safely treat as assigned; no particular assignment mechanism is specified here.
So a partition cannot turn one tenant’s quota into a full quota on each side?

Correct. Connectivity loss does not multiply quota ownership. Each disconnected scheduler remains bounded by its assigned quota, while the broader nonduplication requirement still applies to the tenant’s quota.
Is the latency target about overall scheduler throughput?

No. It is specifically about unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers. Good aggregate throughput or an acceptable average dispatch latency would not, by itself, show that this p99 requirement is met.
How should I read the 2× comparison?

Compare an unaffected tenant’s p99 dispatch latency on a healthy worker with that tenant’s workload-matched isolated baseline. The target is at most 2× that baseline. “Workload-matched” matters: an isolated measurement for a different workload would not be the stated comparison.
Does the target apply to every worker and tenant in every condition?

Its stated scope is healthy workers and unaffected tenants. It should not be silently broadened into a claim about unhealthy workers or affected tenants. At the same time, the design goal includes migration, adversarial workloads, and network partitions; those conditions do not, by themselves, erase the stated target for healthy workers and unaffected tenants.
What role do adversarial workloads play in the requirement?

They are part of the conditions the scheduler must withstand while preserving performance isolation. An adversarial workload must not cause unaffected tenants on healthy workers to exceed the stated p99 dispatch-latency bound. The goal does not specify a particular adversarial behavior, so the requirement should not be narrowed to one assumed pattern.
Could I describe the design as successful if quota ownership is safe, even when another tenant’s dispatch latency rises sharply?

Not on quota safety alone. The design must also keep unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline. Conversely, a good latency result would not excuse duplicated quota ownership or a disconnected scheduler exceeding its assigned quota.
Can you state the conditions as concise design invariants?

Yes:

- A tenant’s quota ownership never duplicates, including through migration, crashes, and network partitions.
- A disconnected scheduler never exceeds its assigned quota.
- On healthy workers, each unaffected tenant’s p99 dispatch latency stays within 2× its workload-matched isolated baseline.

The first two constrain quota ownership and use; the third constrains performance isolation.
Does “never duplicates” allow the system to discover and repair duplicate ownership later?

No. Later repair would not satisfy a rule that ownership never duplicates. The design needs the nonduplication property to hold throughout the relevant events, not merely after migration completes or connectivity returns.
And if a disconnected scheduler stays under its own quota, is that sufficient for quota safety?

It is necessary but not sufficient. The scheduler must stay within its assigned quota, and quota ownership must not duplicate. A per-scheduler limit cannot substitute for the ownership rule if two schedulers can both treat the same quota as theirs.

For the distributed scheduler, I propose consensus-backed escrow credits with expiry-gated lease transfers, worker-enforced fencing, and per-tenant dispatch lanes using weighted fair queuing. Can you unpack how these pieces fit together?

They address different parts of the design. Consensus-backed escrow credits provide an authoritative basis for which quota has been assigned. Expiry-gated lease transfers constrain when ownership can move, rather than treating a migration request or loss of contact as permission for both sides to act. Worker-enforced fencing puts an authority check at the point where work is dispatched. Per-tenant dispatch lanes with weighted fair queuing address interference between tenants. The pieces are complementary: quota ownership and enforcement do not, by themselves, provide latency isolation, and queue isolation does not establish quota safety.
What does “escrow” mean here, without assuming a particular implementation?

It means treating assigned quota as bounded credits that a scheduler may use without obtaining fresh permission for each action. “Consensus-backed” means the authoritative allocation of those credits is grounded in a shared agreement, rather than in each scheduler’s independent view of what it owns. The proposal does not specify the credit size, accounting interval, or consensus protocol.
Is that intended to let a scheduler keep working through a partition?

It can allow a disconnected scheduler to act within credits already assigned to it. Disconnection is not a source of additional credits, though: it must not exceed its assignment or treat credits assigned elsewhere as its own. Whether and how much work it can continue dispatching depends on the valid assignment available to it.
Why include expiry-gated lease transfers if the credits are consensus-backed?

Authoritative credit assignment and safe transfer are related but distinct questions. Expiry gating expresses a constraint on the handoff: the receiving side cannot simply treat an old owner’s silence as proof that its authority has ended. A transfer must respect the lease’s expiry condition so that migration does not create overlapping claims to the same quota. The proposal names that constraint without specifying lease durations or a transfer protocol.
If the old scheduler crashes during migration, should the new one take the credits immediately?

Not merely because the old scheduler appears to have crashed. An apparent crash could also be a communication failure, and the ownership rule does not allow duplicate authority in either case. Under the proposed approach, the new side’s ability to use transferred quota remains subject to the expiry-gated transfer and the authoritative credit assignment; the precise handoff steps are not specified.
How does worker-enforced fencing contribute if schedulers already track leases?

It places a check at the worker, where a stale scheduler might otherwise still get work accepted. Conceptually, a worker should not accept a dispatch on the strength of an ownership claim that has been fenced off. Scheduler-side bookkeeping alone would not provide that enforcement if a scheduler is delayed, disconnected, or operating on an outdated view. The proposal does not prescribe a particular fencing-token format or validation mechanism.
So fencing is not the same thing as reducing the old scheduler’s credit count?

Right. Credit assignment bounds what a scheduler is authorized to use; fencing addresses whether a worker accepts a dispatch made under an old or otherwise invalid claim. They reinforce one another but answer different questions. Neither should be described as a substitute for the expiry condition on transfers.
Could the worker accept dispatches from both schedulers during a migration as long as neither exceeds its local counter?

Local counters alone would not answer whether the two schedulers are using distinct assigned credits or both claiming the same quota. The proposal is aimed at avoiding that ambiguity: consensus-backed assignment defines the credits, expiry-gated transfers constrain the change in ownership, and worker-enforced fencing prevents acceptance under a fenced claim. A migration must preserve nonduplicated quota ownership throughout, not just leave both schedulers individually below some local count.
Where do the per-tenant dispatch lanes enter the picture?

They separate tenants’ pending dispatch work so one tenant’s queue does not simply become the shared queue for everyone. Weighted fair queuing is the proposed policy for allocating dispatch opportunities across those lanes. That is the performance-isolation side of the design, particularly relevant when one tenant presents an adversarial workload.
Does weighted fair queuing guarantee the p99 target on its own?

No guarantee follows from naming the policy alone. The target remains that, on healthy workers, unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency stays within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline. Per-tenant lanes and weighted fair queuing are proposed means of limiting interference, but the proposal supplies no weights, operating conditions, or evidence from which to conclude that the numerical target is met.
What does the weighting commit us to? Equal treatment of every tenant?

It commits the proposal to weighted fair queuing, not to a particular set of weights or equal weights. The essential distinction here is that dispatch opportunities are managed across tenant-specific lanes under a weighted-fair policy, rather than allowing one tenant’s backlog to dictate the entire shared dispatch order. No numerical allocation among tenants is stated.
Could an adversarial tenant still create a large backlog in its own lane?

Yes, a lane can contain a backlog. The point of separating lanes is that such a backlog need not automatically put an unaffected tenant’s work behind all of the adversarial tenant’s work in a single undifferentiated queue. Whether the complete system preserves the specified p99 bound still has to be established; the proposal does not claim that lanes eliminate every possible source of dispatch delay.
How should I think about quota and queuing together? Is a fair turn equivalent to quota ownership?

No. A fair turn concerns scheduling order or service among tenant lanes. Quota ownership concerns how much a scheduler is authorized to dispatch on a tenant’s behalf. A tenant might receive a turn under the queueing policy without that turn granting any new credits. Conversely, holding credits does not entitle a tenant to bypass the dispatch-lane policy.
In a partition, could fair queuing compensate for uncertainty about who owns a tenant’s credits?

No. Weighted fair queuing can manage contention among work that is eligible for dispatch; it cannot resolve conflicting ownership claims or enlarge a disconnected scheduler’s assignment. Consensus-backed credits, expiry-gated transfers, and worker-enforced fencing are the proposed quota-safety components. The per-tenant lanes address performance interference separately.
What if the receiving scheduler can reach a worker but cannot reach the old scheduler?

Reachability alone should not confer ownership. In that situation, the receiving scheduler would still need authority consistent with the consensus-backed credit assignment and the expiry-gated transfer, and the worker’s fencing check would still matter. The proposal intentionally does not infer from an unreachable old scheduler that its lease has expired or its claim is safe to replace.
Is there a specific lease length, credit amount, or fencing scheme implied by this proposal?

No. It specifies the architectural ingredients and their roles, not those parameters or a concrete protocol. Any detailed design would have to make their interactions precise enough that migration, crashes, and partitions cannot duplicate quota ownership, disconnected schedulers stay within assigned quotas, and the latency objective for unaffected tenants on healthy workers can be assessed. Those properties are requirements to preserve, not outcomes already demonstrated by naming the ingredients.
What lease-expiry and worker-fencing protocol prevents overlapping quota spending during partitioned migration without indefinitely stranding credits?

That is the unresolved protocol question. It has to establish both when the old scheduler’s authority ends and when the receiving scheduler may safely use the credits. During a partition, inability to contact the old scheduler cannot by itself answer either question. Workers must also enforce the boundary: a scheduler with a stale claim must not be able to spend credits after those credits have become available to another scheduler. At the same time, the boundary needs a way for credits to become usable again after the old authority has ended, rather than requiring contact with an old scheduler that may never return. No exact expiry rule or fencing procedure has been specified yet.
Why isn’t waiting for the lease to expire enough?

Expiry can define when an ownership claim ends, but it does not, by itself, tell us what every worker will accept. A partitioned scheduler might still present a claim to a worker operating on an outdated view. The protocol has to make lease expiry and worker enforcement agree, so that making credits available to the receiving side does not leave an old path for spending the same credits.
And why isn’t worker fencing enough without an expiry rule?

Fencing can stop a worker from accepting a claim that is no longer valid, but it does not alone establish when the credits may change owners. If transfer depends indefinitely on hearing from the old scheduler, a partition or crash could leave credits stranded. The open question is how to make the end of the old claim determinable while ensuring workers reject its subsequent use.
Suppose the receiving scheduler can reach some workers, while the old scheduler can reach others. What has to remain true?

Reachability must not divide one quota into two spendable copies. Before and after any transfer, the schedulers’ accepted dispatches must remain consistent with nonduplicated ownership and their assigned credits. The protocol must account for workers reachable from either side, not just the workers visible to the scheduler initiating migration.
Could the new scheduler start spending at the nominal expiry instant?

That would be safe only if the protocol defines expiry in a way both sides and the enforcing workers can apply without an overlap. A nominal time written in a lease is not a complete answer unless its interpretation, and the treatment of an old claim presented afterward, are clear. The question does not supply those rules, so it does not establish that spending may begin at any particular instant.
What about work the old scheduler dispatched just before its authority ended?

That is one of the boundaries the protocol must define. It needs to distinguish whatever spending was validly authorized before the handoff from attempts to spend the same credits after the old authority ends. Otherwise, a delayed message could look like new spending at a worker even though the old scheduler sent it earlier. The question identifies the need for worker fencing but does not settle how such in-flight work is accounted for.
Does preventing duplicate ownership mean stopping all dispatch during a partition?

Not necessarily. A disconnected scheduler may use credits that remain validly assigned to it, without exceeding that assignment. What it cannot do is infer extra authority from the partition, and another scheduler cannot begin using the same credits while the old claim remains spendable. The exact conditions under which dispatch continues are part of the protocol to be worked out.
I also don’t want safety to mean that migrated credits are unusable forever.

Right. The liveness side of the question is that a crashed or unreachable old scheduler should not be an indefinite prerequisite for reusing credits once its authority has safely ended. But a finite recovery claim needs stated conditions: for example, the protocol must have a dependable way to determine that expiry has taken effect and to enforce fencing where dispatches could be accepted. Without such conditions, neither immediate transfer nor an unconditional promise of eventual reuse is justified.
So ‘the old scheduler did not respond’ is not evidence that it stopped spending, but requiring its acknowledgment could strand credits?

Exactly. Silence does not prove that its authority has ended; it might be partitioned and still able to reach a worker. Yet an acknowledgment-only handoff could wait indefinitely if the old scheduler cannot respond. The lease-expiry and fencing protocol has to bridge those two constraints without letting both sides spend overlapping quota.
Where do the consensus-backed escrow credits enter this specific question?

They provide the proposed authoritative basis for what credits are assigned. The lease-transfer rule would have to say when an assignment may change, and worker fencing would have to prevent acceptance under an invalid old claim. Consensus-backed allocation alone does not settle what happens at expiry or what a partitioned worker accepts; those are precisely the protocol details in question.
Would a fencing check only at the receiving scheduler be sufficient?

No. It would not constrain a partitioned old scheduler that never consults the receiving scheduler. The proposal calls for worker-enforced fencing because acceptance at a worker is the point that matters for preventing stale dispatches from spending transferred credits.
Can we state the essential handoff test without choosing a concrete mechanism?

Yes: at every point in a partitioned migration, ask whether a dispatch from each side could be accepted against the same credits. If both could, the handoff has not prevented overlapping spending. Then ask whether, after the old claim has safely ended, there is a path for the credits to become usable without waiting forever for that old scheduler. The proposed lease-expiry and worker-fencing protocol must answer both questions; this node does not yet specify the mechanism or demonstrate that it passes either test.

Here is a hypothesis for the partitioned-migration handoff: with ≤2-second clock skew, epoch-fenced workers and reassignment after 30-second leases expire plus skew prevent overlapping quota spending and bound how long credits are stranded.

That is a proposed answer to the handoff question, not yet an established result. The 30-second lease sets a period of authority; waiting for expiry plus skew is intended to keep reassignment from overlapping that authority under the ≤2-second clock-skew assumption. Epoch-fenced workers are intended to reject dispatches made under an older ownership claim once the new one is in force. Together, those measures aim both to prevent two schedulers from spending the same credits and to make the credits reusable after a bounded wait.
Why does the hypothesis need both the wait and the worker fence?

They cover different parts of the handoff. The expiry-plus-skew rule constrains when credits can be reassigned. Fencing concerns what workers accept if an old scheduler continues sending dispatches, perhaps because it is partitioned and has not learned of the reassignment. Waiting without enforcement could leave an old dispatch path open; fencing without a safe reassignment point would not establish when the new claim may begin.
Does a 30-second lease mean the receiving scheduler can spend the credits 30 seconds after it asks for them?

Not as stated. The hypothesis says reassignment occurs after the 30-second leases expire plus skew. It does not define expiry as 30 seconds after a migration request. The relevant lease’s expiry, and the added skew allowance, are the conditions it proposes for reassignment.
Since skew is at most 2 seconds, should I call this an exact 32-second handoff?

I would not infer an exact handoff time from the hypothesis alone. It states ≤2-second clock skew and reassignment after a 30-second lease expires plus skew, but does not specify how the skew allowance is calculated, where the timing begins, or how reassignment reaches workers. The claim is that stranding is bounded, not that every migration completes in exactly 32 seconds.
What is the epoch doing in ‘epoch-fenced workers’?

Conceptually, an epoch distinguishes an older ownership claim from a later one so that a worker can fence the older claim. Its purpose here is to make the ownership change enforceable where dispatches are accepted. The hypothesis does not specify how epochs are assigned, conveyed to workers, or checked, so those details cannot yet be treated as settled.
If the old scheduler stays partitioned, could it keep presenting its old epoch?

It could continue presenting an old claim; the point of worker-enforced fencing is that presenting it must not be enough to spend reassigned credits. For the hypothesis to hold, workers that can accept the relevant dispatches must enforce the transition so an old epoch cannot remain spendable alongside the new one. Whether the proposed arrangement achieves that in every partition is still a question to examine.
What if a worker has not learned that a newer epoch exists?

That is an important case. Merely issuing a newer epoch somewhere would not, on its own, prevent a worker with an outdated view from accepting the older one. The handoff must relate reassignment to what workers can actually enforce, including workers reachable by the old scheduler during a partition. The hypothesis names epoch-fenced workers but does not spell out that coordination.
Does expiry plus skew make the worker’s outdated view harmless?

That is what needs to be established, rather than assumed. The timing rule is meant to separate the old lease’s authority from reassignment despite ≤2-second clock skew. The fencing rule is meant to stop acceptance under an old epoch. To conclude there is no overlapping spending, their definitions must line up at the worker, including around expiry; the stated hypothesis does not provide that full protocol.
Suppose an old dispatch was sent before expiry but arrives at a worker after reassignment. Which epoch should the worker accept?

The hypothesis does not specify how to treat that in-flight dispatch. It illustrates why ‘sent before expiry’ and ‘accepted after reassignment’ cannot be conflated. A complete protocol would need an acceptance and accounting rule that preserves nonoverlapping spending even for delayed messages; we cannot infer that rule just from the lease duration and the presence of epochs.
Is the ≤2-second skew a measured result or an assumption of this hypothesis?

It is an assumption stated in the hypothesis. The proposed safety and bounded-stranding claims are conditional on clock skew being ≤2 seconds. Nothing in the hypothesis establishes that the bound holds in an actual deployment, or says what happens if it is exceeded.
And ‘bounded stranding’ means the credits cannot be stuck waiting forever for the old scheduler to acknowledge migration?

That is the intended contrast. Reassignment after lease expiry plus skew would not make an old scheduler’s acknowledgment the sole way to release credits. But the hypothesis does not give an unconditional time-to-reuse guarantee under every communication failure: the bound depends on the timing assumption and on reassignment and worker fencing being able to take effect as required.
Would repeatedly renewed leases change the stranding claim?

They could affect when a lease expires, so a claim about a bounded wait would need to say which expiry governs reassignment. This hypothesis gives a 30-second lease length and says to reassign after expiry plus skew; it does not describe renewal or specify how renewal interacts with migration. I would not silently add a renewal rule to its claim.
Can we separate what this hypothesis claims from what it still leaves open?

It claims that, assuming ≤2-second clock skew, epoch-fenced workers and reassignment after 30-second leases expire plus skew prevent overlapping quota spending while bounding credit stranding. It leaves open the precise expiry interpretation, the skew allowance, the worker’s epoch-enforcement behavior, and the treatment of delayed dispatches. Those details matter to determining whether the claimed safety and bounded wait follow.
Does the hypothesis also establish the unaffected-tenants’ p99 dispatch-latency target?

No. This hypothesis addresses lease transfer, quota spending, and stranded credits during a partitioned migration. The separate target remains that, on healthy workers, unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency stays within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline. Nothing in this lease-and-fencing hypothesis establishes that latency outcome.
If a partition persists beyond the lease expiry, is the claim simply that the new side takes the credits anyway?

The proposed reassignment point is after the 30-second lease expires plus skew, rather than after the partition heals. But ‘takes the credits anyway’ omits the essential safety condition: workers must not also accept spending under the old claim. The hypothesis proposes epoch fencing for that purpose; it does not demonstrate how every relevant worker is brought across the boundary during a continuing partition.
So I should frame it as a conditional protocol hypothesis, not a proven guarantee?

Yes. State the ≤2-second clock-skew assumption, the 30-second leases and expiry-plus-skew reassignment condition, and the epoch-fenced worker requirement explicitly. Then present prevention of overlap and bounded stranding as the hypothesized consequences, while leaving their validity open until the expiry and worker-acceptance rules are made precise.

I want to turn the lease-and-fencing idea into a concrete plan: specify 30-second leases, expiry-plus-skew reassignment, worker epoch fencing, and TLA+ checks for overlapping credit use across crashes and partitions.

That plan has a protocol-specification part and a checking part. The specification needs to make clear when a 30-second lease grants authority, when its expiry plus the skew allowance permits reassignment, and what epoch-fenced workers will accept. The TLA+ checks should then look for executions in which the same credits can be used under overlapping claims, including executions with crashes or network partitions. Planning those checks is not the same as having run them or established the safety property.
What should ‘30-second lease’ say beyond the duration?

The duration alone does not define a handoff. The specification needs an unambiguous meaning for the lease’s start and expiry, and for what a scheduler is authorized to do while that lease is valid. It also needs to identify the point after expiry plus skew at which reassignment becomes permissible. Those definitions matter most near the boundary, where an old dispatch and a new assignment might otherwise both appear valid.
Does expiry-plus-skew mean the receiving scheduler may reassign credits as soon as it stops hearing from the old scheduler?

No. Silence is not expiry. Under this plan, reassignment is gated on the 30-second lease expiring and the skew allowance being accounted for. A crash or partition may explain why the old scheduler cannot respond, but neither event by itself authorizes an early transfer.
Should we state a particular number of seconds for the skew allowance here?

This plan names expiry-plus-skew reassignment but does not itself give a numerical skew allowance. To specify the rule precisely, the assumed skew bound and how it is applied would have to be stated. I would not derive an exact reassignment time from the 30-second lease duration alone.
What exactly must the worker-fencing part specify?

It needs to say how a worker decides whether a dispatch’s epoch is authorized for the credits it would use, particularly around a transfer. The critical behavior is that an old epoch must not remain an accepted way to spend credits while a new epoch is also accepted for those same credits. The plan calls for worker epoch fencing; it does not yet supply the acceptance rules that would make that statement precise.
Could we leave worker behavior implicit and just check the schedulers’ assignments in TLA+?

That would leave out a central part of the proposed safety mechanism. An old scheduler might continue sending dispatches during a partition, so the question is not only what assignments schedulers believe they hold, but also what workers can accept. A check for overlapping credit use should account for worker acceptance under epochs, not merely compare the schedulers’ local records.
When you say ‘overlapping credit use,’ are we checking only whether two schedulers have the same lease written down?

No. Duplicate lease records would be one concern, but the planned TLA+ checks are for overlapping *use* of credits. A useful formulation asks whether an execution lets an old claim and a reassigned claim both authorize accepted spending against the same credits. That keeps the check focused on the ownership-safety requirement rather than on records alone.
Which failures belong in those checks?

The plan explicitly calls for crashes and partitions. Their ordering matters conceptually: a scheduler might crash during a transfer, or a partition might leave the old scheduler able to reach some workers while the receiving scheduler reaches others. The checks should not assume that every participant sees a failure or a reassignment at the same time. That is a description of what the planned checks need to cover, not a claim that any such cases have been modeled yet.
Would a delayed dispatch sent under the old lease be relevant?

Yes. The specification needs to distinguish when a dispatch was sent from when a worker accepts it. A message sent before expiry could arrive after reassignment, and the fencing rule must determine whether accepting it would overlap use of the reassigned credits. That is a natural boundary case for the planned checks, without presupposing which acceptance rule the protocol will choose.
How do we keep the model from treating a partition as permission to grant fresh credits on both sides?

Make credit assignment and reassignment explicit in the specification, rather than deriving authority from connectivity. The check can then ask whether partitioned executions ever allow two accepted uses of the same assigned credits. A disconnected scheduler remains limited to its assigned quota; losing contact does not create another allocation.
Is there also a reason to model a crash just before expiry versus just after it?

Yes. Those timings probe the boundary between the old lease’s authority and any later reassignment. A crash before expiry must not silently shorten the lease in a way that creates overlap; a crash after expiry should not be treated as proof that workers have fenced the old epoch. The intended safety property has to hold regardless of where the crash falls relative to expiry.
Do the TLA+ checks establish that credits cannot be stranded indefinitely?

Not from the checks stated in this plan. They are specifically checks for overlapping credit use across crashes and partitions. Expiry-plus-skew reassignment is intended to provide a route to reuse without waiting indefinitely for the old scheduler, but a separate, precisely stated progress question would be needed to assess when reassignment and usable dispatch can actually occur. We should not present a safety check as proof of that progress claim.
So if a check finds no overlapping use, can I declare the handoff safe?

Only within the behavior and assumptions represented by the specification and the TLA+ check. In particular, the lease timing, skew assumption, reassignment rule, worker fencing, crashes, and partitions must be represented accurately enough for the result to speak to the intended handoff. The current node is a plan to specify and check those things; it reports no completed check or result.
Does this plan include testing the p99 dispatch-latency requirement?

No. This plan is about lease expiry, credit reassignment, worker fencing, and TLA+ checks for overlapping credit use across crashes and partitions. The separate performance target for unaffected tenants on healthy workers is not measured or verified by those safety checks.
Can you phrase the planned safety question in one sentence?

Under the specified 30-second leases, expiry-plus-skew reassignment, and worker epoch-fencing rules, is there any crash-or-partition execution in which the same credits can be used under overlapping old and new claims? That is the question the proposed TLA+ checks are meant to probe, not an answer they have already supplied.
Let’s model-check LeaseFence.tla with three schedulers, epoch-fenced workers, 30-second leases, ±2-second skew, crashes, and partitions. I want to check both overlapping credit use and stranding.

That activity puts the lease-and-fencing hypothesis under examination rather than assuming its conclusion. The overlap check asks whether old and new claims can both lead workers to accept spending against the same credits. The stranding check asks whether credits can remain unusable indefinitely after the conditions for their release should be satisfied. The three-scheduler model should allow more than a simple handoff between two schedulers to be considered; no outcome of either check is stated yet.
Why be explicit about three schedulers instead of just saying ‘multiple schedulers’?

Three is the stated scope of this model-checking activity. It makes clear what LeaseFence.tla is to be checked with, without implying that a result for three schedulers automatically covers every possible scheduler count. It also keeps the discussion of possible ownership claims from silently assuming that only an old owner and one receiving scheduler exist.
What role do the workers have in an overlap check?

The relevant question is whether a worker can accept a dispatch that spends credits under an epoch that should be fenced. Comparing scheduler claims alone could miss that acceptance behavior. For overlap, the check needs to distinguish a scheduler presenting an old claim from a worker actually accepting credit use under it while another claim is spendable.
Does ‘epoch-fenced workers’ tell us the precise acceptance rule?

No. It identifies the behavior to represent: workers enforce an epoch boundary against stale claims. LeaseFence.tla must give that idea precise semantics for a check to be meaningful, but this activity description does not specify the rule or say that it has already been shown sufficient.
Should the 30-second lease be treated as a performance target?

No. Here, 30 seconds is the lease duration in the protocol being model-checked. It is relevant to when authority expires and when credits might be eligible for reassignment. It is not a claim about dispatch latency, migration completion time, or the time any particular worker takes to receive an update.
And why include ±2-second skew in this activity?

It makes the timing uncertainty explicit in the model-checking conditions. A lease-expiry rule has to remain safe when relevant clocks differ within the stated ±2-second skew. The check can then probe whether the modeled timing and fencing rules permit overlapping use near the expiry boundary. Stating that skew range does not itself establish safety.
Could we just check a handoff at the nominal expiry time?

That would leave out the timing variation the activity explicitly includes. The point of modeling ±2-second skew is to examine behavior around the boundary, not just one nominal ordering. The overlap and stranding questions both depend on when authority is considered ended and when another scheduler can act.
What kinds of behavior do ‘crashes and partitions’ require us to consider?

They require the checks not to assume uninterrupted communication or that a scheduler remains available throughout a lease or transfer. In particular, a partition can leave participants with different views, while a crash can interrupt a handoff. The model-checking activity is to examine overlap and stranding under those conditions; it does not report which executions occur or what any check finds.
If an old scheduler is partitioned, does its inability to hear about reassignment make its dispatch harmless?

No. Whether a dispatch is accepted by an epoch-fenced worker is what matters for credit use. A partitioned scheduler may still present its old claim, so the overlap check should not equate lack of communication with lack of possible spending. Likewise, the stranding question cannot simply assume the old scheduler will respond to release the credits.
How is ‘stranding’ different from overlap in this check?

Overlap is a safety concern: the same credits must not become spendable under conflicting claims. Stranding is a progress concern: credits should not remain unavailable indefinitely merely because migration was interrupted or a participant cannot be contacted. A behavior that avoids overlap by never making the credits usable again would still raise the stranding question.
Does checking stranding mean demanding immediate reassignment after a crash?

No. The activity includes 30-second leases and ±2-second skew, so a wait associated with expiry is not the same as indefinite stranding. The check needs a precise account of when credits could become eligible for reuse; it should not treat a crash alone as permission for immediate reassignment.

Not from the lease duration alone. The leases were 30 seconds and the model included ±2-second skew. Is 34 seconds simply 30 plus two seconds on each side?

The reported bound is 34 seconds, but the result does not give a derivation of that number. The 30-second leases and ±2-second skew identify modeled conditions; they do not, by themselves, specify the timing origin or justify a particular arithmetic explanation of the 34-second finding.

What if a credit was reassigned but could not yet be spent at a worker?

I’ve decided to adopt 30-second epoch-fenced leases with quorum-backed expiry-plus-skew transfers. The adoption is contingent on enforcing the clock-skew bounds and having workers reject stale epochs.

That is a conditional design decision. What does “quorum-backed” add to the transfer rule?

It means the expiry-plus-skew transfer is not authorized solely by one scheduler’s local judgment that the lease has ended. The decision calls for quorum backing for that transfer. It does not specify how the quorum records or communicates the change, so I would leave those mechanics open rather than imply a particular protocol.
If the old scheduler cannot be reached during migration, may the receiving scheduler claim the credits immediately?

No. Unreachability is not the adopted transfer condition. The decision calls for a quorum-backed transfer after the 30-second lease expires plus the skew allowance. An old scheduler’s silence cannot replace either the timing condition or quorum backing.
Why retain an expiry wait if workers will reject stale epochs?

The two conditions have distinct roles. Expiry plus skew governs when the transfer may be made; worker fencing governs whether dispatches under an old epoch are accepted afterward. Rejecting stale epochs does not, by itself, authorize an early transfer of credits that remain under a valid lease.
Could we instead rely on the expiry wait and omit the worker check?

That would not be this decision. Worker rejection of stale epochs is an explicit contingency of adoption. The transfer rule and the enforcement rule must work together: a transferred claim should not become spendable while workers can still accept spending against the same credits under an old claim.
Does ‘epoch-fenced lease’ mean a scheduler can keep using an old epoch until it personally learns about a newer one?

No such exception is stated. The important enforcement point is the worker’s decision to accept or reject a dispatch. A scheduler might present an old epoch because it has not learned of a transfer, but the adoption is contingent on workers rejecting stale epochs; the scheduler’s lack of notice does not make that epoch current again.
What if a worker has not learned enough to tell whether an epoch is stale?

That is a question the concrete worker rule must answer before the contingency can be considered satisfied. The decision requires rejection of stale epochs; it does not specify how a worker obtains the information needed to make that determination. We should not silently assume that every worker has the necessary view at the right time.
Does ‘enforced clock-skew bounds’ mean we can just configure clocks and trust them?

The word “enforced” is stronger than merely choosing a clock configuration. The decision depends on the skew staying within the bounds used by the expiry-plus-skew transfer rule. It does not prescribe a method for maintaining or checking that condition, so the particular enforcement mechanism remains unspecified.
Should I state an exact number of seconds after a migration request when credits transfer?

No exact time after a request follows from this decision. It specifies 30-second leases and transfers after lease expiry plus skew, with quorum backing. It does not define the transfer interval as starting when a migration request is made, nor does it state that acquiring quorum is instantaneous.
Could a crash shorten the lease so that we transfer earlier?

A crash is not stated as an exception to the adopted expiry-plus-skew rule. Treating an apparent crash as early expiry would change the decision and could confuse unreachability with the end of authority. The stated transfer condition remains expiry plus skew, backed by quorum.
And if quorum is unavailable when the lease expires?

The decision still calls for a quorum-backed transfer, so expiry by itself is not enough. It does not promise that credits can be reassigned while the required quorum is unavailable. That limits what can be claimed about progress during such a partition, even though the design is intended to avoid overlapping ownership.
Is there a conflict between refusing transfer without quorum and wanting credits not to remain stranded?

There is a tradeoff to describe precisely, but the decision does not remove its conditions to make transfer faster. It permits reassignment through an expiry-plus-skew, quorum-backed path rather than requiring an acknowledgment from the old scheduler; it does not guarantee progress when quorum cannot back the transfer. We should preserve that distinction rather than promise unconditional availability.
What must remain true at the worker when the new epoch becomes usable?

A worker must reject a stale epoch rather than allow it to spend the transferred credits alongside the new claim. That is the worker-fencing contingency at the heart of this decision. The exact ordering and acceptance semantics at the boundary still need to be specified; the decision does not supply a message format or an in-flight-dispatch rule.
If a dispatch was sent under the old epoch before expiry but arrives afterward, does this decision say whether to accept it?

Not by send time alone. The decision requires workers to reject stale epochs, but it does not define precisely how acceptance of an in-flight dispatch is determined at the transfer boundary. The concrete rule must keep old and new claims from producing overlapping spending without inventing an exception for a delayed message.
Does the quorum grant new credits to compensate for any that are temporarily unavailable?

No such credit creation is part of the decision. Quorum backs the expiry-plus-skew transfer of quota ownership; it is not a license to duplicate credits while a lease is unresolved. A disconnected scheduler remains limited to its assigned quota.
How should I state the decision without making it sound like we have already completed the implementation?

You could say: “Adopt 30-second epoch-fenced leases and quorum-backed transfers after lease expiry plus skew, contingent on enforced clock-skew bounds and workers rejecting stale epochs.” That states the choice and its conditions without claiming that those conditions have already been implemented or that every operational case has been resolved.
Does adopting the lease protocol also mean the performance-isolation part of the scheduler is settled?

No. This decision is about quota ownership and transfer enforcement. It does not establish the separate requirement that, on healthy workers, unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency stay within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline. Per-tenant dispatch isolation remains a distinct aspect of the scheduler.
What is the main caveat I should repeat when discussing the adopted handoff?

That adoption is contingent on both enforced clock-skew bounds and worker rejection of stale epochs. The 30-second lease and quorum-backed expiry-plus-skew transfer should not be presented as independently sufficient if either contingency is absent.
What does LeaseFence.tla actually specify for this handoff?

LeaseFence.tla specifies quorum-backed lease transfers, expiry-plus-skew guards, and epoch-fenced worker admission. It also contains invariants for credit ownership and stranding. That identifies the parts represented in the artifact, though it does not give the exact formulas, state variables, or transition definitions.
What is the distinction between a lease transfer and a worker admitting a dispatch?

A lease transfer concerns which scheduler has authority over the credits. Worker admission concerns whether a particular dispatch is accepted under the epoch it presents. LeaseFence.tla represents both sides of that boundary: changing an ownership claim and enforcing it where work could be admitted.
Why specify the quorum condition in the transfer rather than only in a description outside the model?

If quorum backing is part of the intended transfer rule, representing it in the specification makes it a condition of the modeled transfer, rather than an informal assumption about what a scheduler will do. The artifact is described as specifying quorum-backed transfers; the description does not say how quorum is represented internally.
Does quorum backing mean any scheduler that sees an expired lease can transfer its credits?

No. An expired lease and a quorum-backed transfer are distinct conditions, and LeaseFence.tla also specifies expiry-plus-skew guards. Its description does not authorize a scheduler to infer a transfer solely from its own view of expiry.
What does the expiry-plus-skew guard contribute?

It makes the timing boundary an explicit constraint on reassignment. The intent is not to treat the first apparent expiry on one clock as automatically sufficient; the skew allowance is part of the guard. The artifact description does not provide the guard’s exact expression, so I would not infer a particular timestamp calculation from its name.
Is worker admission just another name for assigning ownership?

No. Ownership identifies the authority to use credits; admission determines whether a worker accepts an attempted dispatch. Epoch-fenced worker admission is important because an old scheduler may still present a claim after a transfer. Specifying admission separately lets the model express whether that attempted use is rejected, rather than assuming an ownership change automatically stops messages from reaching workers.
What does the epoch establish at that point?

It distinguishes a claim made under an earlier authority from one made under a later authority, so the worker can apply fencing when deciding whether to admit work. The supplied description does not define the epoch representation or the precise comparison a worker performs.
Could the artifact include an ownership invariant but omit the worker rule and still capture the concern?

It would not capture the same specified handoff behavior. A statement about who owns credits does not by itself say whether workers accept dispatches presented under stale epochs. LeaseFence.tla is described as including epoch-fenced worker admission as well as credit-ownership invariants, so both the claimed authority and its enforcement are within the artifact’s stated scope.
What should I understand by ‘invariants for credit ownership’?

They are formal conditions about how credit ownership is allowed to appear in the specified states. The central concern is avoiding conflicting ownership of the same credits. The description says those invariants are present, but does not provide their exact definitions or tell us to equate any particular formula with every aspect of accepted credit spending.
And what does it mean to have invariants for stranding?

Stranding concerns credits remaining unavailable rather than being transferred into a usable assignment. The artifact is described as having invariants for stranding, but without their formulas we cannot say precisely how it represents that concern. In particular, an unconditional claim that credits cannot remain stranded forever would require careful treatment of the conditions under which progress is possible; the artifact description alone does not supply that claim.

Not generally. An invariant ordinarily constrains states that can be reached, while ‘eventually’ is a temporal progress claim.
