You can say: ‘LeaseFence.tla specifies quorum-backed lease transfers with expiry-plus-skew guards, epoch-fenced admission of dispatches by workers, and invariants concerning credit ownership and stranding.’ That describes the artifact without supplying unstated formulas or making a new claim about all possible executions.
Does the file name tell us what workers do when they receive a delayed dispatch?

No. The relevant part is the stated epoch-fenced worker-admission specification, but the artifact description does not show its rule for a delayed dispatch. We can say that worker acceptance is modeled; we cannot reconstruct a particular in-flight-message rule just from the file name or the list of components.
Can I say the expiry-plus-skew guard fences the old scheduler?

I would keep the roles separate. The expiry-plus-skew guard constrains when a lease transfer is permitted; epoch-fenced worker admission governs whether a dispatch under an old claim is accepted. Both are specified in LeaseFence.tla, but a timing guard alone should not be described as the worker’s fencing check.
Could the stranding invariant be used as a substitute for the credit-ownership invariant?

No. They address different failure modes. A rule about credits not being stranded would not, by itself, rule out conflicting ownership; a rule about nonconflicting ownership would not, by itself, ensure credits can be reassigned. LeaseFence.tla is described as containing invariants for both concerns.
Does this artifact specify weighted fair queuing or the per-tenant dispatch lanes too?

Not according to this description. LeaseFence.tla’s stated contents concern lease transfers, expiry-plus-skew guards, worker epoch fencing, credit ownership, and stranding. It does not specify the performance-isolation policy or establish the p99 dispatch-latency target for unaffected tenants on healthy workers.
Is there enough here to reproduce the TLA+ specification from our conversation?

No. The artifact’s responsibilities are identified, but its state variables, actions, formulas, and checking configuration are not given in this node. We can explain what LeaseFence.tla covers without inventing source code or claiming an exact formalization we have not been shown.

For the next model-checking activity, extend LeaseFence.tla with in-flight dispatches and asymmetric partitions. Then model-check per-tenant credit conservation and stale-epoch rejection during migration.

That extends the handoff model in two directions: dispatches may be delayed between a scheduler sending them and a worker deciding whether to admit them, and connectivity need not look the same to every participant. The checks then have two distinct targets. Per-tenant credit conservation asks whether migration, including those delayed dispatches, can create or lose credits in the modeled accounting. Stale-epoch rejection asks whether workers refuse dispatches presented under an epoch that is no longer authorized. This is an activity to carry out, not a reported check result.
Why is an in-flight dispatch different from a dispatch that has already been admitted?

An in-flight dispatch has been sent but has not yet received the worker’s admission decision. Ownership might change during that interval. The model needs to distinguish the act of sending from the act that could use credits at the worker; otherwise it cannot examine which epoch the worker accepts when a delayed dispatch arrives during migration.
Is the important case a dispatch sent before a transfer and delivered afterward?

That is a useful general boundary case. Its send time and admission time can fall on opposite sides of a migration boundary. The check should determine whether the specified worker rule rejects a stale epoch at admission and whether the tenant’s credits remain properly accounted for. The activity does not yet state what the model checker finds for that case.
Does adding in-flight messages mean every delayed dispatch must be rejected?

No. The target is rejection of stale epochs, not rejection of all delayed messages. Whether a particular epoch is stale must follow from the specified migration and worker-admission rules. The model needs to make that distinction rather than equating message delay with invalid authority.
What makes a partition asymmetric in this context?

It means the model cannot assume that all participants have the same connectivity or learn about a transfer together. A scheduler and a worker might be able to exchange a message while other participants cannot. The activity does not prescribe a specific partition topology; it calls for the checks to include unequal communication paths during migration.
Why does that matter for worker fencing?

Because a worker’s admission decision is local to that worker, while a migration can change which epoch is authorized. Under asymmetric connectivity, it would be unsafe to reason only from what the receiving scheduler knows or from what one worker has heard. The stale-epoch check should examine admission decisions wherever a dispatch can arrive, including from a scheduler operating with a different view of the migration.
Are we changing the quorum-backed lease-transfer rule by modeling asymmetric partitions?

The activity does not say to change that rule. LeaseFence.tla specifies quorum-backed transfers and expiry-plus-skew guards; extending it with asymmetric partitions lets the checks examine those specified rules when communication paths differ. It does not make a scheduler’s local view of the network a substitute for quorum backing.
Could the model just record a credit balance for the whole cluster?

That would not, by itself, express the requested per-tenant conservation check. The accounting has to distinguish tenants so that credits attributed to one tenant cannot silently appear as another tenant’s credits, even if a cluster-wide total stays unchanged. The activity does not specify the representation of those balances.
What exactly should ‘per-tenant credit conservation’ mean when a tenant is migrating?

It should express that a transfer changes where a tenant’s credits are assigned, not the amount of that tenant’s credits merely by moving them. In-flight dispatches make it important to account consistently for credits that may be reserved, spent, or still subject to a worker’s admission decision—depending on how the specification defines those states. The precise conservation formula needs to come from the model; no formula or credit quantity is supplied here.
If a dispatch is in flight, should its credits count as spent?

That is a definition the extension must make explicit, rather than something this activity settles. Whatever treatment it chooses must not let the same tenant credits be counted as available for a new owner while the in-flight dispatch can also spend them. The check should follow the specified accounting and worker-admission events.
Would rejection of a stale dispatch return credits to the tenant?

The activity does not specify a refund or reservation rule. It calls for per-tenant conservation and stale-epoch rejection, so the extension needs to define how a rejected dispatch affects credit accounting without creating or losing credits. We should not assume a particular return mechanism before that rule is written.
Suppose a delayed dispatch is admitted under an old epoch at one worker while a new epoch is usable elsewhere. Which check notices the problem?

The stale-epoch rejection check addresses whether that worker should have admitted the old epoch. The per-tenant conservation check addresses whether the associated credit accounting permits more use or ownership than the tenant’s credits allow. They examine related aspects of the same migration boundary, but neither check should be silently treated as an exact substitute for the other.
Could conservation pass even if a worker admits a stale epoch?

They are distinct properties, so the model should check both rather than infer one from the other. An aggregate accounting rule might preserve a tenant’s stated credit total while a worker still makes an admission decision the fencing rule forbids. Conversely, correctly rejecting stale epochs does not automatically establish that credits are accounted for correctly through every transfer and in-flight state.
Does stale-epoch rejection mean a partitioned scheduler is forbidden from sending dispatches?

No. Sending and worker admission are different events. A partitioned scheduler might attempt to send under an old epoch; worker-enforced fencing concerns whether the worker accepts it. The model-checking target is rejection at admission when the epoch is stale, not an assumption that old messages can never be sent.
Should asymmetric partitions include the possibility that two workers see different epochs at the same time?

The extension should be able to examine admission under differing connectivity rather than assume a uniform view. Whether and how two workers can hold different epoch information is a matter for the model’s state and transition rules. The crucial question for the requested check is whether any reachable worker admits a dispatch under an epoch that the specified authority rules make stale during migration.
Does ‘during migration’ restrict the checks to the instant of reassignment?

It should not be reduced to one instantaneous snapshot. A migration has a boundary across which transfers, messages in flight, and admission decisions can be ordered differently. The requested checks concern behavior through that boundary, including a dispatch whose sending and admission occur at different points. The activity does not provide an exact migration timeline.
Would these checks establish that a disconnected scheduler never exceeds its assigned quota?

They are relevant to that safety requirement, but their stated targets are per-tenant credit conservation and stale-epoch rejection during migration. Whether they fully establish the disconnected-scheduler quota bound depends on what the extension models and what properties are checked. No outcome, or claim that these two checks exhaust every quota rule, is given here.
Can this extension also tell us how quickly stranded credits are reassigned?

Not just from the two checks named here. Conservation and stale-epoch rejection are about accounting and admission safety. A time-to-reassignment or progress bound would need its own stated property and assumptions. Extending the model with in-flight dispatches and asymmetric partitions does not itself supply a new stranding result.
What about per-tenant dispatch lanes and weighted fair queuing—are they part of this model-checking activity?

They are not named in this extension. This activity concentrates on credit conservation and stale-epoch rejection during migration, with in-flight dispatches and asymmetric partitions. It does not evaluate weighted fair queuing or whether unaffected tenants on healthy workers meet the p99 dispatch-latency target of within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline.
Is there a concise way to describe the proposed checks without claiming they passed?

Yes: “Extend LeaseFence.tla to represent in-flight dispatches and asymmetric partitions, then model-check whether tenant credits are conserved and workers reject stale epochs throughout migration.” That states the work and the properties to examine, without reporting a result.
What is the key modeling pitfall to avoid when adding in-flight dispatches?

Do not collapse sending, arrival, worker admission, and credit accounting into one event if their separation is what exposes the migration boundary. The extension needs enough distinction to ask whether a message sent under one claim can be admitted after that claim becomes stale, and whether its tenant’s credits remain conserved either way. This identifies the question the model should represent, not a particular implementation or a finding.
The extended LeaseFence.tla check found a 17-step partition trace. An in-flight old-epoch dispatch survived reassignment, and the trace consumed 101/100 credits concurrently. What does that show?

It is a counterexample to the intended credit-safety behavior in the extended model. In that 17-step partition trace, reassignment did not prevent an in-flight dispatch under the old epoch from contributing to concurrent consumption of 101 credits against 100. The proposed lease-transfer and worker-fencing arrangement, as represented in this trace, therefore does not suffice to prevent overlapping credit use in that case.
Is 101/100 just a notation for the ownership change?

No. It reports credit consumption: 101 credits were consumed concurrently against a limit of 100. The important point is not merely that two ownership claims appeared, but that the trace reached spending beyond the available credits.
Does the 17-step length matter to the conclusion?

It identifies the counterexample as a 17-step partition trace. The safety failure is the in-flight old-epoch dispatch surviving reassignment and the resulting 101/100 concurrent credit consumption. The step count does not, by itself, say how long the failure lasted in real time.
When you say the dispatch was in flight, what distinction matters?

The dispatch was already in progress while authority could change. Its old epoch did not stop it from surviving reassignment in the reported trace. That distinguishes this case from considering only dispatches newly initiated after reassignment; the handoff must also account for work already in flight.
Does the result tell us that the old scheduler deliberately ignored a newer epoch?

No. The reported trace identifies an in-flight old-epoch dispatch, not the scheduler’s intent or what it knew. The counterexample does not require an adversarial decision by the old scheduler to be significant: delayed work can cross the reassignment boundary regardless of intent.
Can we say worker fencing failed?

We can say the modeled fencing arrangement did not prevent this old-epoch dispatch from surviving reassignment and contributing to excess concurrent consumption. The result does not isolate a specific worker-rule defect or show exactly which admission decision needs to change. Those would require examining the trace and the model’s rules in more detail.
Could the issue instead be credit accounting rather than epoch rejection?

The observation implicates their interaction: an old-epoch in-flight dispatch survived reassignment, and concurrent consumption reached 101/100. The stated evidence does not identify whether the decisive gap lies in admission, accounting, the transfer boundary, or a combination. What it establishes is that the represented rules together permit this outcome.
Why is a single credit over the limit enough to matter?

Because the requirement is not an approximate limit. Consuming 101/100 credits concurrently demonstrates that the 100-credit bound was exceeded in the reported trace. A one-credit excess is still a counterexample to a rule that must hold without exceptions.
Does this prove that quota ownership duplicated?

The reported counterexample directly establishes excess concurrent credit consumption. It does not separately state how the model labeled ownership in that state. I would describe the observable failure as overlapping credit use or a breach of credit conservation, rather than substitute an unstated ownership-invariant result.
How does the partition figure in the finding?

The counterexample is explicitly a partition trace, so the failure occurs in the partitioned behavior represented by the extended LeaseFence.tla model. The evidence does not specify the partition’s exact connectivity pattern; it would be unwarranted to name which scheduler or worker could reach which other participant.
Can I conclude every partitioned migration will exceed its quota?

No. The trace establishes that at least one modeled partitioned migration can reach 101/100 concurrent credit consumption. It does not say that every partition produces the failure, or how often it would occur outside the model. One reachable counterexample is nevertheless enough to refute an unconditional claim that the modeled arrangement always prevents overlapping spending.
Does this counterexample say anything about the 30-second lease duration or the skew bound?

Not beyond the context of the extended LeaseFence.tla check. The reported finding is about an in-flight old-epoch dispatch surviving reassignment during a 17-step partition trace. It does not give timestamps, identify a clock-skew violation, or attribute the excess consumption to a particular lease duration.
Should I describe this as credits being stranded?

No. Stranding means credits remain unavailable for use. Here the reported problem is the opposite kind of safety failure: credits were consumed concurrently beyond the 100-credit limit. This finding does not report a new stranding duration or outcome.
Does the trace settle the scheduler’s p99 dispatch-latency goal?

No. It concerns migration, epochs, partitions, and credit consumption. It supplies no measurement of unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers against their workload-matched isolated baselines.
What is the narrow conclusion about the proposed consensus-backed escrow and fencing design?

In the extended model, the proposed combination does not prevent this partitioned-migration counterexample: an in-flight old-epoch dispatch survives reassignment and concurrent consumption reaches 101/100 credits. That challenges the proposal’s sufficiency for quota safety as modeled. It does not identify a particular repair or establish anything about the weighted-fair-queuing component.
Can you give me a concise statement of the finding without guessing the root cause?

“Extended LeaseFence.tla found a 17-step partition trace in which an in-flight old-epoch dispatch survived reassignment, allowing concurrent consumption of 101/100 credits.” That reports the counterexample without assigning an unreported cause or fix.
Can in-flight old-epoch dispatches overspend escrow credits after asymmetric partitions and lease reassignment?

They can if an old-epoch dispatch remains capable of consuming credits after those same credits have been reassigned and made spendable under a new epoch. The key boundary is worker admission, not just when the old scheduler sent the dispatch. The question is whether the lease-transfer, fencing, and credit-accounting rules together exclude that overlap under asymmetric connectivity.
Why does it matter that the dispatch was already in flight?

Because stopping a scheduler from sending *new* old-epoch dispatches does not settle what happens to one it sent earlier. That dispatch may reach a worker after reassignment. If the worker can admit it against credits that the receiving scheduler can also spend, sending it before the handoff has not made the accounting safe.
Should I count a dispatch as credit use when it is sent or when the worker admits it?

The protocol needs an explicit accounting rule for those distinct events. Counting at send time might require a way to keep the in-flight amount unavailable during transfer; counting at admission time requires admission to respect the current credit authority. The question does not prescribe either choice. What matters is that no choice permits the same tenant credits to be available for reassignment and for an in-flight dispatch to consume.
What does an asymmetric partition add to the problem?

It prevents us from assuming that the old scheduler, receiving scheduler, and every worker share the same view at the same time. A message sent under the old epoch might still reach a worker even though a transfer is proceeding elsewhere. The safety rule must hold across those differing communication paths, rather than relying on all participants learning of reassignment together.
Does lease expiry alone make an old-epoch dispatch harmless?

Not automatically. Expiry governs authority, but an in-flight message can still arrive at a worker. The worker’s admission decision and the credit accounting must ensure that a dispatch under expired authority cannot consume credits that are now spendable under a reassigned claim. Merely declaring a lease expired does not describe what the worker will do.
And does a newer epoch automatically fence every older message?

Only if the worker-admission rule actually rejects the older epoch where that message can be accepted. Assigning a new epoch somewhere is different from establishing how a worker treats a delayed old-epoch dispatch. The question asks whether that distinction leaves a path to overspend during reassignment.
If the old dispatch arrives after reassignment, must the worker reject it even if it was sent while the old lease was valid?

Its earlier send time does not, by itself, make later admission safe. The protocol must decide which authority governs admission and how any credits associated with the in-flight dispatch were accounted for during transfer. A rule that accepts it must still prevent concurrent spending of those same credits under the new assignment; otherwise it permits the overspend in question.
So the issue is not simply that two schedulers hold different epoch numbers?

Right. Different epoch numbers can appear during a handoff without, by themselves, showing excess use. The safety question is whether a worker accepts spending under the old epoch while the reassigned credits can also be spent under the new epoch. It is the combination of admission and credit availability that matters.
Could per-tenant credit conservation catch an overspend even if an ownership record looks unique?

That is why it is useful to ask about accepted credit use as well as recorded ownership. A unique ownership record does not by itself account for an in-flight dispatch that a worker may later admit. Per-tenant conservation should examine whether all uses and assignments of that tenant’s credits remain within the available amount across the transfer.
Does the partition create additional escrow credits?

No. A partition changes communication, not the amount of a tenant’s escrow credits. If the old side can still spend an in-flight dispatch while the same credits are available to the receiving side, the resulting excess would come from overlapping access to credits, not from a legitimate increase in their assignment.
Would it be enough to check that the old scheduler never initiates a dispatch after its lease expires?

No. That check would miss dispatches initiated earlier but admitted later. The question specifically concerns in-flight old-epoch dispatches surviving an asymmetric partition and lease reassignment. A meaningful check has to represent the interval between sending and worker admission.
How should I phrase the precise safety question for a model check?

Ask whether any migration execution with asymmetric connectivity permits an in-flight dispatch under the old epoch to be admitted after reassignment in a way that makes accepted use of a tenant’s escrow credits exceed that tenant’s available credits. That formulation keeps the focus on admission, reassignment, and per-tenant accounting without presuming which rule is responsible.
If a stale dispatch is rejected, does that alone answer the conservation question?

Not entirely. Rejection addresses whether that particular old-epoch dispatch can consume credits. Conservation also requires consistent accounting for credits associated with dispatches in flight, admitted, or rejected as ownership changes. The checks are related, but a worker-admission rule and a credit-accounting rule need to agree.
What if the receiving scheduler waits until expiry plus skew and obtains quorum backing—can overspend still be the question?

Yes. Those conditions govern when reassignment is permitted; the question also asks what happens to old-epoch dispatches that were already in flight and can reach workers under asymmetric connectivity. A permitted transfer must not make credits spendable twice merely because the old message was sent before the transfer.
Is this about the latency-isolation target too?

No. This question concerns quota safety during migration: whether old-epoch in-flight dispatches can cause escrow-credit overspending after an asymmetric partition and reassignment. It does not measure unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers against their workload-matched isolated baseline.
What is the essential distinction to keep in mind while examining it?

Separate the old scheduler’s authority to send, a message’s time in flight, the worker’s authority to admit it, and the reassigned credits’ availability to the new owner. The overspend question arises if those events can be ordered so that the same tenant credits support accepted use on both sides of the handoff.

I propose transferring only reconciled unused credits. In-flight reservations would remain held until worker-confirmed completion or enforced execution expiry plus a clock-skew margin. How does that address the migration handoff?

It separates credits known to be unused from credits still committed to a dispatch whose outcome is unresolved. Only the reconciled unused portion would be eligible for transfer. An in-flight reservation would remain unavailable for reassignment until worker-confirmed completion establishes its outcome, or until the execution expiry has been enforced and the clock-skew margin has passed. The proposal is intended to prevent a delayed dispatch from consuming credits that have already been made available to another scheduler; it is not yet a demonstrated guarantee.
What does “reconciled” add to “unused”?

It means the transfer decision should be based on an accounted state, not simply on a scheduler’s belief that it has not recently sent work. A credit might look unused locally while a dispatch using it is still in flight. Reconciliation has to distinguish such reserved credits from credits that are actually available to transfer. The proposal does not specify the reconciliation procedure.
Could we transfer everything that has not yet been admitted by a worker?

Not under this proposal. A dispatch that has not yet been admitted may still arrive and be accepted. Its reservation remains held while that possibility is unresolved. Treating ‘not yet admitted’ as ‘unused and transferable’ would collapse the distinction this proposal is trying to maintain.
Is an in-flight reservation itself a second quota owner?

The proposal treats it as an outstanding claim on credits, not as a new allocation to another scheduler. Its practical importance is that the same reserved credits must not also appear in the reconciled unused amount offered for transfer. The exact representation of ownership and reservations remains to be specified.
What happens when the worker confirms completion?

Confirmation gives the reconciliation process an outcome for that dispatch, so its reservation need not remain unresolved. That does not automatically make the reserved credits unused: any credit consumption associated with the completed work still has to be accounted for. Only credits that are unused after reconciliation qualify for transfer.
Why say worker-confirmed completion rather than relying on the sending scheduler’s record?

The scheduler’s record that it sent a dispatch does not establish what happened at the worker. Worker-confirmed completion supplies an outcome from the place where the work was handled. The proposal names that confirmation as one way to resolve an in-flight reservation, without specifying a confirmation message or an accounting format.
If a scheduler crashes before receiving that confirmation, can migration simply free the reservation?

A scheduler crash is not one of the stated release conditions. The reservation remains held until worker-confirmed completion can resolve it or enforced execution expiry plus the clock-skew margin provides the other specified boundary. A crash alone would not show that the dispatch can no longer consume the credits.
Does the same reasoning apply when a partition prevents the confirmation from arriving?

Yes. Missing confirmation during a partition is uncertainty, not evidence that the credits are unused. The proposal keeps the in-flight reservation out of the transferable amount until one of its stated resolution conditions applies.
What does “execution expiry” mean here? Is it just expiry of the lease being transferred?

The proposal specifically says *execution* expiry for resolving an in-flight reservation. That is a boundary on the outstanding dispatch’s ability to consume its reserved credits, whereas a lease-transfer boundary concerns reassignment of quota authority. The proposal does not define either timer in terms of the other, so lease expiry alone should not be treated as release of an in-flight reservation.
Why must execution expiry be enforced?

If a dispatch could still be accepted or consume the reserved credits after its nominal execution expiry, that expiry would not safely resolve the reservation. The proposed alternative to worker-confirmed completion depends on expiry being effective, not merely on a timestamp having passed in one participant’s view.
And what is the clock-skew margin for?

It accounts for uncertainty when different clocks are used to interpret the execution-expiry boundary. The proposal requires holding the reservation through enforced expiry *plus* that margin, rather than releasing it at one observer’s apparent expiry instant. It does not specify a numerical margin or how clocks are checked, so an exact release time cannot be inferred.
Could the receiving scheduler use all the other unused credits while one reservation is still unresolved?

That is the distinction the proposal makes: transfer only the portion that has been reconciled as unused, while continuing to hold the in-flight reservation. It does not require treating every credit as transferable merely because migration has begun, nor does it say one unresolved dispatch must automatically make all other credits unavailable.
If the worker confirms completion, should the receiving scheduler get those reserved credits immediately?

Not simply because confirmation arrived. First the outcome and any associated consumption have to be reconciled. The transfer rule still applies only to credits found to be unused. Confirmation resolves uncertainty about the dispatch; it is not, on its own, a grant of credits to the receiving scheduler.
What if the execution expires while a message is still in transit to the worker?

The expiry path is safe only if the execution-expiry rule is enforced against such a message, with the clock-skew margin observed before the reservation is released. Otherwise a late arrival might still consume credits after those credits become transferable. The proposal identifies the required boundary but does not spell out the worker’s admission rule for every in-flight message.
Does this replace epoch fencing during migration?

The proposal does not say that it does. Holding reservations and transferring only reconciled unused credits address which credits may move while dispatches are unresolved. Epoch fencing addresses whether a worker admits a dispatch under a stale authority claim. Those concerns can interact, but this proposal does not declare either one a substitute for the other.
Could reconciliation show that all credits are reserved, leaving nothing to transfer yet?

Yes, that follows from transferring only reconciled unused credits: if none have been established as unused, this rule would not make any eligible for transfer. The proposal favors keeping unresolved reservations held over guessing that they are free. It does not give a bound on how long every reservation will remain unresolved.
Does enforced execution expiry prevent credits from being stranded indefinitely?

It proposes a way to resolve an outstanding reservation without waiting solely for worker-confirmed completion. A definite progress claim would depend on execution expiry actually being enforceable, the skew margin being applied, and reconciliation and transfer being able to proceed. The proposal does not state an unconditional time bound or establish what happens if those conditions cannot be met.
How should the accounting treat a credit while it is held for an in-flight dispatch?

It must not count that credit as part of the reconciled unused amount available for transfer. The proposal leaves open the exact accounting states and whether eventual completion records consumption or expiry releases a reservation. In either case, reconciliation must determine what remains unused before those credits can be transferred.
Is this a proposal about per-tenant dispatch latency as well?

Its stated focus is credit transfer and in-flight reservations during migration. It does not specify dispatch-lane scheduling or show whether unaffected tenants on healthy workers keep p99 dispatch latency within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline.
Can you state the proposed handoff rule briefly, without claiming it has already been validated?

Transfer only credits reconciled as unused. Keep credits reserved for in-flight dispatches out of that transfer until worker-confirmed completion resolves them or enforced execution expiry plus the clock-skew margin safely ends their ability to be consumed. Whether those rules fully preserve quota safety and allow timely reuse remains to be established.

I want to implement reservation-aware transfers and per-tenant dispatch lanes, then test credit conservation during partitioned migration and healthy-worker p99 dispatch latency against a ≤2× workload-matched isolated baseline. How do those parts of the plan fit together?

They address the scheduler’s two requirements. Reservation-aware transfers concern quota safety: credits associated with unresolved dispatches must not become available to spend again merely because a tenant is migrating. Per-tenant dispatch lanes concern performance isolation: one tenant’s pending work should not automatically determine another tenant’s place in the dispatch queue. The planned tests examine credit conservation under partitioned migration and whether, on healthy workers, unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency stays at or below 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline. The plan does not report either outcome yet.
What makes a transfer reservation-aware?

It accounts for credits committed to in-flight dispatches separately from credits established as unused and eligible to move. The transfer must not make a reserved credit spendable by the receiving side while the outstanding dispatch can still consume it. The plan calls for implementing that distinction; it does not specify the data structures or a completed accounting rule.
Does implementing transfers mean moving every credit as soon as migration starts?

No. Reservation awareness is specifically a reason not to treat all credits as immediately transferable. The amount eligible to move depends on what has been reconciled as unused, while unresolved reservations remain accounted for. Migration starting is not, by itself, proof that an in-flight dispatch can no longer spend its credits.
How do per-tenant dispatch lanes relate to those reservations?

They solve different problems. Reservations constrain credit availability across a handoff; lanes organize pending dispatch work by tenant to limit cross-tenant interference. A tenant having work in its lane does not create new credits, and having available credits does not remove the need to consider how its work shares dispatch capacity with other tenants.
Is the plan saying that lanes alone will guarantee the p99 target?

No. The lanes are an implementation step, and the healthy-worker p99 comparison is a test. The plan does not claim that creating lanes is sufficient to keep unaffected tenants within the ≤2× threshold. That is what the performance test is meant to assess.
What exactly is being conserved in the partitioned-migration test?

Tenant credits must remain consistently accounted for as they are reserved, used, or transferred. A migration across a partition must not make the same credits available for spending on both sides or create extra spendable credits. The plan calls this a credit-conservation test; it does not provide a formal accounting equation or report a result.
Would checking the total number of credits across all tenants be enough?

Not for a tenant-quota requirement. An unchanged cluster-wide total could conceal credits being attributed to the wrong tenant. The conservation test needs to respect tenant boundaries as well as the transfer boundary, though this plan does not prescribe its exact measurement or model.
Why specify partitioned migration instead of just an ordinary transfer?

A partition can leave participants with different information while dispatches and a migration are in progress. Testing conservation in that condition probes whether credits remain properly accounted for without assuming that every scheduler and worker learns about the transfer together. The plan does not specify a particular partition layout.
Should the test assume that the old scheduler stops sending as soon as migration begins?

That assumption would avoid an important part of the quota-safety question. Reservation-aware transfers are intended to account for outstanding work, not depend on all activity stopping at the start of migration. The plan does not prescribe a particular workload sequence, but the test should be capable of examining whether unresolved dispatches and transferred credits can overlap.
If a credit remains reserved, does conservation require that it also be counted as available to the new scheduler?

No. Counting the same credit as both reserved for an outstanding dispatch and available to the receiving scheduler would undermine the purpose of reservation-aware transfers. Conservation requires consistent accounting across those states, not simultaneous availability on both sides.
Does the credit-conservation test also prove that a disconnected scheduler stays within its assigned quota?

It is relevant to that requirement, but the plan names partitioned-migration credit conservation as the test target. Whether a particular test fully covers every way a disconnected scheduler might exceed its assigned quota depends on the cases and accounting it includes. The plan does not claim comprehensive proof of the disconnected-scheduler bound.
How should we read the p99 comparison precisely?

For an unaffected tenant on a healthy worker, compare its observed p99 dispatch latency with its workload-matched isolated baseline. The target is that the former is no more than 2× the latter. The comparison is about the tail of dispatch latency, not average latency or overall throughput, and the isolated baseline must match the workload being compared.
Could we use one isolated baseline for every tenant to simplify the test?

Not unless it genuinely provides the workload-matched isolated baseline for each comparison. The stated criterion is not a single arbitrary reference latency shared across unlike workloads. The plan does not supply baseline values or a method for obtaining them.
Why limit the performance comparison to healthy workers and unaffected tenants?

Those are the stated conditions of the latency requirement. The test should retain them rather than quietly change the claim to all workers or all tenants. It should also not narrow the requirement to average behavior among unaffected tenants if an individual tenant’s p99 is the quantity being compared.
Would a low average dispatch latency establish that the p99 result is acceptable?

No. The target is specifically p99 dispatch latency. An average can look acceptable while a tenant’s tail latency exceeds 2× its workload-matched isolated baseline. The planned performance test has to make the p99 comparison itself.
Do we need to test performance while another tenant has an adversarial workload?

Adversarial workloads are part of the broader scheduler goal, so they matter to the intended isolation claim. This plan states a healthy-worker p99 test for unaffected tenants but does not define a particular adversarial workload or a test configuration. We can keep the isolation objective in view without inventing a specific workload for this node.
Does an unaffected tenant mean its own quota or work cannot change during the test?

The plan uses ‘unaffected tenants’ to identify whose latency must meet the comparison; it does not give a detailed operational definition or say that every characteristic of their workload is fixed. Workload matching still matters when choosing each isolated baseline. We should not add a stricter eligibility rule without one being specified.
Could credit conservation pass while p99 latency fails?

Yes. Accurate quota accounting does not establish performance isolation. Likewise, acceptable p99 dispatch latency would not establish that credits are conserved through partitioned migration. That is why the plan includes both the conservation test and the healthy-worker latency comparison.
Could the per-tenant lanes themselves change how quota ownership is transferred?

The plan does not say that they do. Lanes concern dispatch organization; reservation-aware transfers concern the credits that authorize dispatch. An implementation must keep those concerns consistent, but a lane should not be treated as a new owner or source of quota merely because it contains pending work.
If a tenant’s lane has queued work while its credits are reserved elsewhere, what can the plan tell us?

It tells us not to confuse queued work with spendable quota. The presence of pending work does not establish that credits are available after a transfer. The exact eligibility and admission behavior for such queued work is not defined by this plan, so I would not infer a dispatch decision from the lane alone.
Are we committing to a specific lane weight or dispatch algorithm in this implementation plan?

This plan says to implement per-tenant dispatch lanes but gives no weights or detailed lane-selection rule. The focus of its stated performance check is the resulting p99 dispatch latency relative to the workload-matched isolated baseline, not an assumed numerical allocation among lanes.
What would count as meeting the latency criterion, numerically?

For any comparison within the stated scope, an unaffected tenant’s p99 dispatch latency on a healthy worker would have to be ≤2× its workload-matched isolated baseline. If that baseline were represented by B, the threshold would be 2B. That illustrates the comparison without supplying an actual measured baseline or test result.
And what would a conservation failure mean in the migration test?

It would mean the tested credit accounting does not preserve the tenant’s quota through the partitioned handoff—for example, if a credit remains spendable through an unresolved dispatch and is also made available after transfer. That is an illustration of the property being tested, not a claim that this implementation has produced such a failure.
Can I describe this as an implementation and validation plan rather than a completed solution?

Yes. The plan is to implement reservation-aware transfers and per-tenant dispatch lanes, then test partitioned-migration credit conservation and compare unaffected tenants’ healthy-worker p99 dispatch latency against the ≤2× workload-matched isolated threshold. It specifies what to build and assess, without asserting that the implementation or tests are complete or that either requirement has been met.

I want to extend LeaseFence.tla with in-flight reservations and worker-enforced execution expiry, then model-check credit conservation across partitioned migrations. What should this activity examine?

It should examine whether a tenant’s credits remain consistently accounted for while dispatches are in flight and ownership is being transferred across a partition. The extension needs to represent credits held as reservations separately from credits eligible for transfer. It also needs to represent the worker enforcing execution expiry, so expiry is more than a scheduler’s belief that an outstanding dispatch has ended. The model check would then look for partitioned-migration executions that violate credit conservation. This describes the activity, not a result.
Why make an in-flight reservation explicit in LeaseFence.tla?

Without an explicit reservation, the model could treat a credit as unused during the interval between sending a dispatch and resolving what happens at the worker. That would obscure whether the same credit can be made available through a migration while the dispatch can still consume it. Representing the reservation lets the conservation check account for that interval.
Does reserving a credit mean the worker has already consumed it?

Not necessarily. A reservation represents an outstanding commitment whose outcome is not yet settled; consumption depends on the model’s admission and accounting rules. The extension needs to distinguish a held reservation from both a credit available for transfer and a credit whose use has been resolved. The activity does not prescribe exact state variables or accounting formulas.
What would be the conservation concern if a transfer occurs while that reservation is held?

The concern is that the reserved credit might be counted again as available to the receiving scheduler while the outstanding dispatch can still use it. A conservation check should detect whether the partitioned migration can make more of a tenant’s credits spendable than that tenant actually has. It should also make clear how a reservation remains accounted for until its outcome is resolved.
Why specify worker-enforced execution expiry rather than just an expiry timestamp in the scheduler?

A scheduler’s timestamp alone does not determine what a worker will admit. If the worker could still accept a dispatch after the execution is supposed to expire, releasing its reservation on the strength of the scheduler’s timestamp could make the credit available twice. Modeling worker-enforced expiry lets the check examine the boundary between an outstanding dispatch’s ability to execute and the release of its reservation.
Is execution expiry the same as expiry of the lease whose credits are being migrated?

No. Lease expiry concerns the authority being transferred; execution expiry concerns the outstanding dispatch associated with a reservation. The extension must not silently treat a lease becoming transferable as proof that an in-flight execution can no longer consume its reserved credit. Both boundaries can matter during migration, but they answer different questions.
If an execution has expired, can the model immediately count its reservation as unused?

The worker-enforcement rule must make that safe. A nominal expiry is not enough if a worker can still accept the associated dispatch. The extension should define when expiry has actually removed that possibility and how the reservation is accounted for afterward. This activity does not state that release is immediate or give a numerical release time.
Would the model need to separate when a dispatch is sent from when the worker sees it?

Yes, to represent an in-flight reservation meaningfully. Sending a dispatch, its possible arrival, and the worker’s decision to admit or reject it can occur on different sides of a migration or execution-expiry boundary. If they were collapsed into one event, the check could miss the interaction it is intended to examine.
How does a partition affect that sequence?

A partition means the participants need not learn about the migration or resolve an outstanding dispatch together. The conservation property should hold even when communication prevents a scheduler from promptly learning what happened at a worker. The activity calls for checking partitioned migrations, without specifying a particular connectivity pattern.
Could we simply assume that no in-flight dispatch reaches a worker once migration starts?

That would remove the situation the extension is meant to model. An in-flight dispatch can remain unresolved across a migration boundary, and partitioned communication makes it especially important not to infer its fate from the start of migration. The reservation and worker-enforced expiry rules need to account for what the worker can actually accept.
What if the worker rejects a dispatch because its execution has expired?

The model would need to reflect both the rejection and its effect on the associated reservation. Rejection should not spend the credit, but the accounting still needs a well-defined way to move from an outstanding reservation to whatever credit state follows. The activity specifies the conservation property to check, not a particular release transition.
And if the worker admits the dispatch before execution expiry?

Then the model needs to account for that use rather than also treating its reserved credit as unused and transferable. The critical conservation question is whether worker admission and transfer can both draw on the same tenant credit. No particular outcome for that case is reported here.
Should this check track credits for each tenant, or would a cluster-wide total suffice?

It should preserve the tenant distinction inherent in quota ownership. A cluster-wide total alone might remain unchanged while credits are misattributed across tenants. Credit conservation across a partitioned migration concerns the migrating tenant’s credits and their reservations, uses, and transfers. The activity does not dictate the model’s exact accounting representation.
Does a held reservation itself count as newly created quota?

No. It accounts for a commitment against existing credits. The same credits should not be counted as both held for an in-flight dispatch and independently available to spend after transfer. The model-checking question is whether the extended rules maintain that accounting across the migration.
What role does the worker play besides rejecting work after execution expiry?

For this extension, worker enforcement supplies the authoritative boundary on whether an outstanding execution can still proceed. That boundary is relevant to when its reservation may be resolved. LeaseFence.tla also represents worker admission, so the conservation check should reflect the consequences of admission or rejection rather than treating every sent dispatch as an accepted use. The exact worker transition rules have to be specified in the extension.
Could the check pass if it simply holds every reservation forever?

Holding reservations forever could avoid one way of double-counting, but it would not explain how worker-enforced execution expiry resolves them. The stated activity is to model that expiry and check conservation, not to claim that a conservation check alone proves credits become reusable promptly. Any progress property would need to be stated and examined separately.
Are we model-checking dispatch latency with this extension?

No. This activity extends LeaseFence.tla to examine credit conservation across partitioned migrations with in-flight reservations and worker-enforced execution expiry. It does not report a healthy-worker p99 dispatch-latency test or a comparison with the ≤2× workload-matched isolated baseline.
Would a successful conservation check, if we eventually obtained one, establish the whole quota-ownership requirement?

It would establish only what the specified property covers within the checked model. Conservation is directly relevant to preventing credits from being counted or spent twice, but the broader requirement also concerns quota ownership through migration, crashes, and partitions, as well as disconnected schedulers staying within assigned quotas. This activity reports no check outcome and does not say its conservation property alone covers every part of that requirement.
What is the essential question to ask at the moment credits are transferred?

For each credit proposed for transfer, ask whether it is still held for an in-flight dispatch that a worker could admit, or otherwise already accounted for as used. If so, counting it as available to the receiving scheduler would put conservation at risk. The extension should make that question expressible in LeaseFence.tla without assuming the answer.
And at the execution-expiry boundary?

Ask whether worker enforcement has actually ended the outstanding dispatch’s ability to consume its reservation before that credit is treated as available again. The model needs to relate worker behavior and reservation accounting at that boundary, including under a partition. Merely advancing a scheduler-side clock would not answer the worker-admission question.
Can you state the activity in one sentence that does not sound like the check is complete?
Extend LeaseFence.tla to represent in-flight credit reservations and worker-enforced execution expiry, then model-check whether tenant credits remain conserved throughout partitioned migrations.
What does LeaseFence-v2.tla specify about credits during a transfer?

LeaseFence-v2.tla tracks credits as spent, reserved, and transferable. It requires worker-confirmed completion or enforced execution expiry before credits held for an outstanding dispatch can be transferred. That makes the dispatch’s unresolved status part of the transfer decision rather than treating every credit not yet recorded as spent as available to move.
Why distinguish reserved credits from spent credits?

A reserved credit is associated with an outstanding dispatch whose outcome still matters to transfer eligibility. A spent credit has been accounted for as used. Keeping those categories distinct lets the specification represent the uncertainty while the dispatch remains outstanding, without calling it either unused and transferable or already spent. The artifact description does not supply the exact accounting formulas.
Is ‘transferable’ simply another word for ‘reserved but not spent yet’?

No. The distinction is the point of tracking the categories separately. A reserved credit is still held for an outstanding dispatch; a transferable credit is eligible to move. LeaseFence-v2.tla requires one of the stated resolution conditions before a held credit can become eligible for transfer.
Could the model treat a credit as reserved and transferable at the same time?

That would defeat the intended separation if it allowed the same credit to support an outstanding dispatch and a transfer. The artifact tracks reserved and transferable credits separately, but its description does not show the precise invariant or transition rule for those categories. We can state the required transfer boundary without inventing its formal expression.
What is the first way an outstanding reservation can be resolved?

Worker-confirmed completion. The confirmation supplies an outcome for the outstanding execution before the associated credit is considered for transfer. It does not mean that a credit consumed by completed work automatically becomes unused or transferable; the specification must still account for spending.
Why does the confirmation have to come from the worker?

The worker is the participant handling the execution, so its confirmation addresses the dispatch’s outcome rather than merely the fact that a scheduler sent it. LeaseFence-v2.tla explicitly names worker-confirmed completion as a condition before transfer. The description does not specify how that confirmation is delivered or recorded.
What is the alternative if worker-confirmed completion is unavailable?

Enforced execution expiry is the other stated condition. The important word is ‘enforced’: the expiry must actually end the outstanding execution’s ability to use the credit before that credit is treated as eligible for transfer. A participant merely assuming that an execution has ended would not express the condition given for this artifact.
Does that mean the model requires both completion and expiry?

No. The condition is worker-confirmed completion *or* enforced execution expiry before transfer. They are alternative ways to resolve an outstanding execution for the purpose of determining whether its reserved credits can move. Neither alternative should be described as permission to transfer credits already accounted for as spent.
Is execution expiry the same event as the lease transfer?

They are distinct concepts. Execution expiry concerns whether an outstanding dispatch can still execute against its reservation. Transfer concerns whether a credit can move to another assignment. LeaseFence-v2.tla requires the relevant execution to be resolved by worker-confirmed completion or enforced expiry before its held credit is transferred; the artifact description does not collapse those events into one.
If an execution has nominally expired, is its reservation immediately transferable?

The stated condition is *enforced* execution expiry, not just a nominal timestamp. Whether and when a credit becomes transferable depends on the specification’s enforcement and accounting rules, which are not shown here. We should not infer immediate transfer merely from a clock reading.
What if a completion confirmation arrives, but the execution spent the credit?

Does this measurement say that quota ownership duplicated during migration?

Does reservation-aware reconciliation delay unaffected tenants’ dispatch beyond 2× isolated p99 under adversarial floods and partitioned migrations?

Quota safety and dispatch latency are separate requirements. The target is within 2× the workload-matched isolated baseline, so exactly 2× is within the stated limit. “Beyond” means greater than 2×. The comparison uses p99 dispatch latency on both sides, not a p99 value compared with an isolated average.
Can I use the isolated p99 of whichever tenant is easiest to measure?

It asks whether unaffected tenants’ dispatch crosses the threshold. A single pooled number could conceal that one unaffected tenant is delayed more than another. Why specify healthy workers?

That is the scope of the latency requirement being examined. Do the flood and partition need to occur at separate times for this comparison?

The wording asks about dispatch under adversarial floods and partitioned migrations. It does not prescribe a timeline or say the conditions must be tested separately. A measurement used to answer it would need to make clear which conditions were present, without inferring an unstated ordering.
Is it enough to show that the scheduler continues dispatching for unaffected tenants?

Would average dispatch latency reveal whether reconciliation delays the tail?

Could quota conservation be maintained while this latency threshold is exceeded?

Should I compare the flooded tenant’s p99 to isolation too?

If I call an unaffected tenant’s matched isolated p99 B, what is the test?

Let P be that tenant’s p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers under the adversarial floods and partitioned migrations. The threshold test is P ≤ 2B. If P > 2B, it is beyond the stated 2× bound. Neither P nor B is supplied by this question.
Does “dispatch latency” include how long an execution runs after a worker admits it?

The stated metric is dispatch latency, not execution duration. The question does not specify detailed timestamp boundaries for measuring dispatch, so it would be inappropriate to add execution time to the metric or assert a particular timing definition here.
If some credits remain reserved through migration, is that necessarily a latency violation?

No. A held reservation is a credit-accounting state, whereas the latency threshold is a comparison of unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch times. Can per-tenant lanes make this question irrelevant?

How should I state the open question without assuming its answer?

“Under adversarial floods and partitioned migrations, does reservation-aware reconciliation push any unaffected tenant’s p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers above 2× that tenant’s workload-matched isolated p99?” That preserves the conditions, the affected metric, and the threshold while leaving the outcome to measurement.
I propose sharding reconciliation locks by tenant and using worker-local weighted fair dispatch, while preserving reservation-aware credit transfers. How do these parts fit together?

The proposal separates the reconciliation work of different tenants and makes dispatch fairness a decision at each worker. Tenant-sharded locks are intended to prevent one tenant’s reconciliation from requiring the same lock as another tenant’s. Worker-local weighted fair dispatch is intended to limit how one tenant’s pending work interferes with another’s at a worker. Reservation-aware credit transfers remain the quota-safety constraint: credits held for unresolved dispatches must not be treated as freely transferable. These are proposed mechanisms, not a demonstrated latency or safety result.
What exactly is sharded by tenant?

The reconciliation locks. Instead of treating reconciliation for different tenants as work under one common lock, the proposal associates locking with the tenant being reconciled. It does not specify the lock representation, how many locks exist, or whether other shared resources remain.
Does that mean two operations for the same tenant can never run together?

The proposal calls for tenant-sharded reconciliation locks, which provides a way to coordinate reconciliation for the same tenant without making another tenant take that same lock. It does not state the exact critical section or define all concurrency permitted within a tenant, so I would not infer a comprehensive serialization rule from the phrase alone.
Is sharding the locks the same as sharding a tenant’s quota?

No. A lock controls access to reconciliation work; quota credits determine what dispatches are authorized. Sharding a lock by tenant does not create credits, divide a tenant’s allocation, or change who owns transferable or reserved credits.
Would an unaffected tenant necessarily avoid all reconciliation delay once the locks are sharded?

Not necessarily. Tenant-specific locks address contention for a common reconciliation lock, but the proposal does not say that every other source of dispatch delay disappears. Whether unaffected tenants meet the p99 dispatch-latency target would still depend on the behavior of the complete scheduler.
Why pair the lock change with worker-local weighted fair dispatch?

They address interference at different points. Tenant-sharded reconciliation locks separate tenants’ reconciliation work; worker-local weighted fair dispatch allocates dispatch opportunities among tenants whose work reaches a worker. Changing only one point would not, by itself, define how the other handles contention. The proposal combines them while keeping the credit-transfer rule intact.
What does ‘worker-local’ qualify in that phrase?

It qualifies where weighted fair dispatch is applied: at each worker. The proposal does not claim a single global dispatch order, nor does it say that local fairness alone establishes a global per-tenant allocation.
Does worker-local weighted fair dispatch mean each worker can assign its own extra credits?

No. Dispatch order and quota authority remain distinct. Weighted fair dispatch determines how a worker selects among eligible tenants’ work; it does not grant a worker or scheduler additional escrow credits. The reservation-aware transfer rule still constrains which credits are available.
What do the weights say about how much service each tenant receives?

Weights are part of a weighted fair dispatch policy, but this proposal provides no weight values or method for choosing them. It specifies the type and location of dispatch policy, not a numerical service share or a guarantee of equal shares.
If one tenant floods a worker with work, does weighted fairness reject all of that tenant’s dispatches?

Not by definition. Weighted fairness concerns how dispatch opportunities are shared among eligible tenants; it is not, on its own, a rule to reject all work from a busy tenant. The proposal is intended to protect other tenants from having their dispatches simply queued behind an adversarial backlog, but it gives no specific admission or rejection rule.
Does a tenant’s turn in the weighted fair policy make its queued dispatch eligible even if the corresponding credit is reserved elsewhere?

No. A turn in dispatch order is not quota authority. The proposed policy must operate on work that is eligible under the credit rules. Preserving reservation-aware transfers means that a credit held for an unresolved dispatch cannot also become spendable for another dispatch merely because its tenant has a fair turn.
What exactly is being preserved from reservation-aware credit transfers?

The distinction between credits established as unused and credits still reserved for outstanding dispatches. Sharding reconciliation locks and making dispatch fair at workers must not cause reserved credits to be counted as transferable or available for a second use. The proposal says to preserve that transfer behavior; it does not specify a new release condition or accounting formula.
Could we remove reconciliation altogether if the worker handles fairness locally?

That is not this proposal. Worker-local fairness addresses dispatch scheduling, whereas reconciliation determines which credits may safely transfer while reservations are outstanding. Keeping reservation-aware credit transfers means the accounting question remains even if dispatch selection happens locally.
Could each worker independently decide which credits are unused for transfer?

The proposal does not grant workers independent authority to reassign credits. It calls for worker-local *dispatch* and tenant-sharded reconciliation locks while preserving reservation-aware transfers. Worker locality in one decision should not be expanded into a new credit-ownership rule.
Suppose two different tenants are being reconciled at once. What is the intended advantage of tenant-sharded locks?

Conceptually, their reconciliation need not contend for the same tenant-specific lock. That is the intended reduction in cross-tenant lock interference. It is not a claim that they are guaranteed to run concurrently, since the proposal does not describe all other constraints on that work.
If the same tenant is migrating during a network partition, do tenant-sharded locks solve ownership ambiguity?

No. Lock sharding addresses contention between tenants, not the authority to spend a tenant’s credits across a partition. The migration must still respect reservation-aware transfers and the broader requirement that quota ownership not duplicate and disconnected schedulers not exceed their assigned quotas.
Do tenant-specific locks mean a tenant gets a separate dispatch lane automatically?

Not automatically. Reconciliation locking and dispatch organization are distinct. The proposal names tenant-sharded reconciliation locks and worker-local weighted fair dispatch; it does not say that the lock itself implements a dispatch lane or describe a particular queue structure.
Can local weighted fairness protect a tenant whose work is on a healthy worker while another tenant is adversarial?

That is the intended performance-isolation role of the policy. It provides a way to share dispatch opportunities at that worker without simply following one combined backlog. Whether it actually keeps an unaffected tenant’s healthy-worker p99 dispatch latency within 2× its workload-matched isolated baseline is not established by the proposal alone.
Is the 2× target an average across healthy workers?

No. The requirement concerns unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers relative to their workload-matched isolated baselines. Averaging away a tail-latency problem would not satisfy that comparison. This proposal gives no p99 measurements.
Could different workers choose different dispatch orders without conflicting with the proposal?

Yes, worker-local dispatch implies decisions are made at workers, so their immediate orders need not be identical. But local order does not override credit eligibility or reservation-aware transfer. The proposal leaves the exact scheduling state and coordination among workers unspecified.
Would sharding locks by worker rather than tenant express the same idea?

No. The proposed sharding key is the tenant. A worker-sharded lock would separate work according to workers, which does not express the same tenant-level separation of reconciliation. The proposal separately puts weighted fair dispatch at workers.
Does the proposal require that a tenant undergoing migration keep receiving the same dispatch share throughout?

It does not specify a share or make a continuity guarantee for the migrating tenant. Weighted fairness describes the proposed worker-local selection policy, while reservation-aware transfer limits which credits are available during migration. Neither statement supplies a measured dispatch share through the handoff.
What if a tenant has a backlog but no currently transferable credits?

A backlog does not make its credits transferable. Worker-local weighted fair dispatch can order work that is eligible to dispatch, but it cannot make a reservation disappear or authorize duplicate spending. The proposal does not define the detailed handling of a lane with pending but ineligible work.
Does this proposal alter the rule for an in-flight dispatch whose completion is not yet known?

No alteration is stated. Preserving reservation-aware credit transfers means unresolved in-flight reservations remain accounted for rather than being counted as unused just because reconciliation or dispatch is organized differently. The proposal does not introduce an exception for missing completion information.
How should I explain the relationship between the safety and performance parts without claiming success?

Say that tenant-sharded reconciliation locks and worker-local weighted fair dispatch are proposed to reduce cross-tenant dispatch interference, while reservation-aware transfers continue to protect credit accounting during migration. The mechanisms are meant to coexist: lowering contention must not make an in-flight reservation transferable, and preserving credits does not alone establish the healthy-worker p99 latency bound.
Can I claim lock sharding will cut p99 latency to a particular value?

No numerical outcome follows from the proposal. It supplies no measured latency, projected reduction, or benchmark result. Its performance aim can be stated in relation to the requirement—unaffected tenants on healthy workers should stay within 2× their workload-matched isolated p99 dispatch latency—but achieving that remains an open question.
Is there a specified number of lock shards or workers?
