No. The ring organizes completion processing; it does not override reservation-aware accounting. A credit held for an outstanding dispatch must be accounted for according to that dispatch’s resolution. The presence or draining of an event is not, by itself, permission to make every associated credit transferable.
Could the adopted arrangement allow a disconnected scheduler to spend beyond its assigned quota in exchange for better latency?

No. Better dispatch latency is not an exception to the quota requirement. The design goal still requires nonduplicated quota ownership and prevents disconnected schedulers from exceeding assigned quotas. The performance components must coexist with reservation-aware transfers rather than relaxing credit authority.
Is this decision just about completion processing, then?

No. It includes reservation-aware reconciliation for transfer accounting, tenant sharding of that reconciliation, per-tenant completion rings, dedicated dispatch cores, and eight-event drains. Those components cover both the credit-transfer path and sources of dispatch interference, while the stated reason concerning 32-event drains is specifically a crash-burst p99 breach.
Do we know from the decision how many cores are dedicated or how many completion rings there are?

No numerical core count or ring count is stated. The decision says the cores are dedicated and the completion rings are per tenant. It should not be expanded into a particular hardware allocation or a specified total number of rings.
Could I describe the eight-event limit as eight events per tenant per tick?

That is how the crash-recovery drain cap was expressed in the proposed arrangement. In the decision itself, the concise term is “eight-event drains.” Neither wording supplies a tick duration, so it should not be converted into an events-per-second rate.
What distinction should remain clear if I discuss the decision with someone focused on quota safety?

The completion rings, dedicated cores, and drain limit organize processing; they do not grant credits or resolve ownership by themselves. Reservation-aware reconciliation remains responsible for keeping unresolved reservations out of transferable credits. The statement that 32-event drains breach crash-burst p99 is a latency judgment, not a new quota-safety finding.
And what distinction matters for someone focused on tail latency?

The relevant performance measure is p99 dispatch latency for unaffected tenants on healthy workers, not average latency, throughput, or completion-processing time. The decision identifies 32-event drains as breaching the crash-burst p99 target and adopts the stated combined arrangement; it does not assign a new numerical p99 to any individual component.
Give me a final concise wording that includes the decision and its stated reason, without adding another result.
“Adopt reservation-aware tenant-sharded reconciliation, per-tenant completion rings, dedicated dispatch cores, and eight-event drains; 32-event drains breach the crash-burst p99 target.”

I propose pairing quorum-certified per-worker quota slices with expiry-fenced reservations and dedicated dispatch cores. During a partition, workers would spend only credits preassigned to them. How do those pieces fit together?

The proposal gives each worker a bounded, quorum-certified slice of quota credits, keeps outstanding reservations subject to expiry fencing, and reserves dispatch cores for dispatch work. The first two components address which credits can safely be spent or remain held; dedicated dispatch cores address interference with dispatch processing. A partitioned worker would spend only credits already assigned to it, rather than treating disconnection as permission to obtain more. This is a proposed design, not a demonstrated safety or latency result.
What is a per-worker quota slice?

It is a portion of quota credits assigned to a particular worker. The important feature here is that a worker’s authority is bounded by its own assignment. The proposal does not specify slice sizes, how many workers receive slices, or how the credits are divided among them.
Does ‘quorum-certified’ mean the worker can decide locally how large its slice is?

No. Quorum certification is the proposed basis for recognizing the assignment; it is not a license for a worker to enlarge its own slice. The proposal does not define the certificate format or the steps by which an assignment is certified.
If two workers lose contact with each other, can each spend the tenant’s full quota?

Not under this proposal. Each partitioned worker is limited to credits preassigned to it. Partitioning does not turn a slice into the tenant’s full allocation or create a second copy of credits assigned elsewhere.
Can a partitioned worker continue dispatching at all?

The proposal permits spending within valid, preassigned credits; it does not require an immediate stop solely because connectivity is lost. If a worker has no credits it can validly treat as preassigned, disconnection does not create any. The proposal does not specify how long a particular slice remains usable or every condition for accepting a dispatch.
Does having a certified slice guarantee that no two workers can claim the same credits?

That is the safety property the assignment and transfer rules would have to preserve, not something established merely by the term ‘certified.’ Certification needs to identify assignments in a way that does not make the same credits simultaneously spendable by two workers, including through migration and partitions. The proposal leaves the exact certification and transfer rules open.
Why add expiry-fenced reservations if each worker already has a bounded slice?

A bounded slice does not settle what happens to credits committed to an outstanding dispatch. Expiry-fenced reservations are meant to keep such credits from becoming available for another use while the original dispatch could still consume them. Slice assignment bounds a worker’s allocation; reservation fencing addresses use and reuse within or across that allocation.
Is the reservation’s expiry the same thing as expiry of a quota slice?

The proposal does not equate them. An expiry-fenced reservation concerns an outstanding claim on credits, whereas a slice concerns the credits assigned to a worker. Treating one expiry as automatically resolving the other would add a rule that is not stated.
What does ‘fenced’ add to the reservation expiry?

It indicates that expiry must be enforced against attempts to use an old reservation, not merely noted by a participant that wants to reuse the credits. Otherwise, credits could be made available again while an outstanding dispatch still has a path to spend them. The proposal does not specify the enforcement mechanism or a numerical expiry period.
If a worker becomes partitioned with an outstanding dispatch, can another worker take its reserved credits immediately?

Not merely because the first worker is partitioned. The outstanding reservation still matters, and the same credits must not become spendable elsewhere while that dispatch can use them. The proposal calls for expiry fencing but does not state the precise conditions under which reserved credits become eligible for reassignment.
Could a worker count a reserved credit as still within its slice while another worker receives it in a new slice?

That would be the overlap the quota design must avoid if both paths could spend the credit. The certification of per-worker slices and the fencing of reservations have to agree on what remains assigned, held, and available to move. This proposal identifies those safeguards without specifying their complete accounting protocol.
Is ‘preassigned’ just a local counter on the worker?

No particular representation is specified. The meaningful constraint is that credits must have been assigned before the worker relies on them during a partition, with quorum certification as the proposed authority for the slice. A worker’s local counter alone should not be mistaken for permission to create or expand an assignment.
Does a quorum need to be reachable for every dispatch from a partitioned worker?

The proposal does not say that. Its partition rule is that workers spend only preassigned credits, which distinguishes using an existing assignment from seeking additional authority. It does not specify a per-dispatch quorum check or exactly when renewed certification would be necessary.
What if a partitioned worker exhausts its preassigned credits?

It cannot exceed that assignment on the strength of being partitioned. The proposal supplies no rule for obtaining additional credits without the needed authority, so an exhausted slice should not be described as automatically replenishing. Whether and when further credits could be assigned is outside the stated proposal.
How does tenant migration affect per-worker slices?

Migration has to preserve the identity and limits of the credits already assigned to workers. Moving tenant scheduling responsibility cannot make a worker’s preassigned slice simultaneously spendable elsewhere, and outstanding reservations cannot be ignored during that move. The proposal does not specify the handoff sequence for slices or reservations.
Do dedicated dispatch cores help establish quota ownership?

No. Dedicated dispatch cores are a performance-isolation component: they reserve processing capacity for dispatch. They do not certify slices, release reservations, or grant additional credits. Quota safety and dispatch latency still need their respective rules and evaluations.
Would dedicated cores guarantee unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency stays within 2× isolation?

Not from the proposal alone. The target remains that, on healthy workers, unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency is within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline. Dedicated dispatch cores are intended to protect dispatch processing, but the proposal supplies no measurement establishing that target under migration, adversarial workloads, or partitions.
Could the worker dispatch work for whichever tenant has the most pending requests, regardless of its slice?

Pending requests do not supply quota authority. Whatever dispatch-order policy a worker uses, it must not spend credits beyond what has been validly preassigned, and it must respect outstanding reservations. This proposal names dedicated dispatch cores but does not define a new dispatch-order policy.
Is a core reservation the same kind of reservation as an expiry-fenced credit reservation?

No. A dedicated core is processing capacity set aside for dispatch; an expiry-fenced reservation is an accounting claim on quota credits associated with work that may still consume them. They have different units and roles. Reserving a core neither resolves a credit reservation nor increases a worker’s slice.
Does the proposal say how many credits or dispatch cores to assign to each worker?

No. It specifies quorum-certified per-worker quota slices and dedicated dispatch cores without numerical slice sizes or core counts. Nor does it give an expiry duration for reservations. Adding those numbers would be a further design choice, not part of this proposal.
What is the most important partition invariant to state?

A partitioned worker spends only credits that were preassigned to it and does not exceed that assignment. Alongside that, assignments and expiry-fenced reservations must not make the same quota spendable twice. The first is the proposal’s explicit partition rule; the second is the ownership-safety requirement it must satisfy.
Could this approach preserve quota safety yet still have poor dispatch latency?

Yes. Bounded, nonoverlapping credit use does not by itself constrain p99 dispatch latency. Conversely, dedicating dispatch cores would not excuse duplicate ownership or overspending. The proposal pairs mechanisms for the two concerns; it does not demonstrate that both requirements have been met.
How would you summarize the proposal without claiming it has been tested?

“Pair quorum-certified per-worker quota slices with expiry-fenced reservations and dedicated dispatch cores, so workers separated by a partition spend only credits preassigned to them.” This states the proposed arrangement and partition limit without asserting a completed verification or latency measurement.
How can quorum-certified slices be reclaimed from partitioned workers without overlapping outstanding reservations?

The central difficulty is that a partitioned worker may be unreachable yet still able to use credits in its certified slice, including credits held for dispatches whose outcomes are unresolved. A quorum’s decision to reclaim a slice cannot, by itself, make those outstanding uses disappear. A safe reclaim rule would have to distinguish credits known to be unused from credits still reserved, and prevent a reclaimed credit from becoming spendable elsewhere while its old use can still be accepted. The question does not yet specify a protocol that establishes those conditions.
Why isn’t it enough for a quorum to certify the slice to a different worker?

Certification establishes an authoritative assignment, but a new certificate alone does not settle what happens to work already authorized under the old assignment. If the partitioned worker or an in-flight dispatch can still spend a reserved credit, making that same credit spendable under the new certificate creates an overlap. Reclamation must account for the old authority and its outstanding reservations as well as the new assignment.
Could we reclaim the whole slice as soon as the worker stops responding?

Silence is not evidence that the worker has stopped spending or that every outstanding dispatch has been resolved. It may be partitioned rather than stopped, and its messages may still reach a worker that can admit them. Reclaiming the whole slice on nonresponse would be safe only if another rule had already made every credit in it unavailable for old use; nonresponse itself does not do that.
What should happen to credits that have no outstanding reservation?

They are the portion to examine for reclamation, but ‘no outstanding reservation’ has to be established through consistent accounting rather than guessed from the reclaiming side’s incomplete view. The safety question is whether each credit proposed for reassignment is actually free of an old spendable claim. The question supplies neither a reconciliation procedure nor a rule for when that determination is authoritative.
Does an outstanding reservation mean the credit has already been spent?

Not necessarily. A reservation indicates that an outstanding dispatch may still consume the credit; spending is an outcome that has to be accounted for. While that outcome is unresolved, the reserved credit cannot safely be treated as unused and simultaneously reassigned. Keeping ‘reserved,’ ‘spent,’ and ‘available to reclaim’ distinct is essential to the question.
Suppose a dispatch was sent before the partition and arrives after the slice is reclaimed. What matters?

What matters is whether a worker can accept that dispatch and charge it to a credit now available under another assignment. Its earlier send time does not make overlapping use safe. A reclaim protocol must account for messages in flight and make the worker’s acceptance behavior agree with the credit accounting at the reclaim boundary.
Would preventing the partitioned worker from sending new work solve that case?

No. Even if it sends nothing new, work already in flight may remain unresolved. The question specifically includes outstanding reservations, so the reclaim rule cannot rely solely on stopping new dispatches; it must address old dispatches that may still be accepted.
Does the quorum need to know the outcome of every outstanding dispatch?

It needs a safe basis for deciding which credits can be reassigned. Knowing an outstanding dispatch’s outcome would be one way to resolve its reservation. If its outcome cannot be established, the credit must remain excluded from reclamation until some enforceable condition ends that dispatch’s ability to spend it. The question does not specify how either condition is established during the partition.
Could expiry provide that enforceable condition?

Potentially, if expiry is enforced wherever the outstanding dispatch could be accepted. Merely observing that a timestamp has passed would not be enough if an old dispatch could still consume the credit. Any expiry-based release would need to establish a nonoverlapping boundary between the old reservation’s spendability and the new slice’s authority; the exact expiry and enforcement rules remain open here.
Is expiry of the worker’s slice automatically expiry of all its reservations?

That does not follow. The slice defines an assignment of credits, while an outstanding reservation represents a possible use of some of those credits. A reclaim rule must say how each reservation is resolved or fenced. It cannot assume that ending the assignment has also made every in-flight dispatch harmless.
What does ‘without overlapping’ require at the instant of reassignment?

For any credit made spendable under the new assignment, there must be no remaining path by which the old worker or an outstanding dispatch can also spend that credit. The rule must hold at the handoff boundary, not just after delayed messages have settled. Otherwise reclamation has produced two simultaneously spendable claims to one credit.
Could the old worker keep spending other credits in its slice during the partition?

The proposal permits a partitioned worker to spend only credits preassigned to it. Reclamation must not retroactively treat credits it can still validly spend as available to someone else. Which credits remain spendable, and when that authority ends, are precisely the boundaries a reclaim protocol has to define.
Does a quorum-backed decision make every worker reject an old reservation immediately?

Not by itself. A decision and enforcement at a worker are distinct events, particularly during a partition. If a worker can still accept an old dispatch, a new certified assignment cannot safely rely solely on the fact that the quorum made a decision. The protocol must connect the decision to what workers will accept, without assuming that all participants learn of it together.
What if one worker can see the new certificate while another can still receive an old dispatch?

Then the credit accounting must not make the same credit spendable through both paths. Different connectivity or different views cannot be allowed to multiply a quota slice. The reclaim rule needs to cover all workers that could accept relevant dispatches, not just the worker receiving the reassigned slice.
Would holding every credit until the partition heals prevent overlap?

It could avoid reassignment while old use remains uncertain, but it would not answer how to reclaim slices from workers that stay partitioned. The question asks for reclamation *without* overlapping outstanding reservations. A satisfactory answer needs a safe way to identify or establish when credits may move, rather than treating connectivity restoration as the only possible resolution.
Is there a difference between reclaiming a slice and reclaiming an individual unused credit from it?

Yes. Reclaiming an entire slice treats all of its credits as eligible to move. Reclaiming only credits established as unused leaves outstanding reservations held back. That distinction may allow a partial transfer without assuming that every dispatch associated with the partitioned worker has been resolved. The question does not yet choose an accounting or certification mechanism for such a transfer.
Can the receiving worker use an outstanding reserved credit if it promises not to use more than its newly certified slice?

A limit on the receiving worker’s own slice is not enough if the certified slice includes a credit that an old dispatch can still spend. Each worker might appear to respect its local assignment while the same credit is available twice. The assignments and the reservation accounting must agree about which particular credits are eligible for reassignment.
Is the issue ownership, spending, or both?

Both are relevant but distinct. Ownership must not duplicate, and the enforcement path must not allow overlapping spending through an old reservation and a new assignment. A clean ownership record alone would be insufficient if a delayed dispatch can still consume a reassigned credit; conversely, temporarily avoiding spending would not justify duplicate ownership.
What is the most careful answer we can give to the original question now?

Quorum-certified slices can be reclaimed safely only to the extent that their credits have been established as unused, or outstanding reservations have been resolved or made unenforceable before those credits become spendable elsewhere. The quorum’s reassignment decision and worker acceptance rules must share that boundary, including during a continuing partition and for dispatches already in flight. The precise protocol for establishing it is the open part of the question; certification or nonresponse alone is not enough.

I want to specify slice-expiry and reservation-settlement guards, then model-check reclamation from partitioned workers before benchmarking dispatch isolation on healthy workers. How should I structure that plan?

Keep the sequence explicit: first define when a worker’s quota slice may expire and when its outstanding reservations are settled; then model-check whether credits can be reclaimed from a partitioned worker without overlapping an old claim; only afterward benchmark dispatch isolation on healthy workers. This is a plan for specification and evaluation, not a claim that reclamation is already safe or that latency meets its target.
Why specify two guards rather than one expiry condition?

Slice expiry and reservation settlement answer different questions. Slice expiry concerns the worker’s authority over assigned credits. Reservation settlement concerns credits already held for outstanding dispatches. An expired slice does not, by itself, establish that every dispatch using its credits has finished or can no longer spend them. The guards need to make the boundary for each kind of claim clear.
What should the slice-expiry guard determine?

It should determine when credits in a worker’s slice cease to be spendable under that assignment and may be considered for reclamation. The plan does not specify a lease duration, clock-skew allowance, or exact expiry rule. Those would need to be defined before a model check could evaluate the intended handoff.
If the worker is partitioned, can its lack of response stand in for slice expiry?

No. A partitioned worker may still be able to act on credits preassigned to it. Nonresponse does not establish that its authority has expired. The slice-expiry guard needs a defined condition that does not rely on mistaking silence for the end of an assignment.
What does the reservation-settlement guard need to protect?

It needs to keep a credit held for an outstanding dispatch from being reclaimed while that dispatch can still consume it. Reclamation should not present the same credit as available to another worker before the old reservation has been resolved or made unable to spend. The plan names a settlement guard but does not yet define its exact events or accounting rule.
Could an expired slice still contain unsettled reservations?

That is a case the specification should be able to represent. Expiry of the slice and settlement of a dispatch need not be assumed to happen together. If a reservation remains unsettled, the reclamation rule must account for it rather than treating every credit in the expired slice as unused.
Does that mean the whole slice must always wait for every reservation?

The plan does not choose between reclaiming a whole slice and reclaiming an eligible portion. What matters to the proposed check is that credits still subject to outstanding reservations do not overlap with credits made spendable under a new assignment. The specification must say which credits a permitted reclamation actually includes.
Is a worker-reported completion necessarily sufficient to settle a reservation?

The guard needs to define what constitutes a settled reservation and how its credit use is accounted for. A completion may resolve an outstanding dispatch, but it does not turn a credit spent by that dispatch into unused quota. This plan does not prescribe a completion message, a release transition, or another specific settlement mechanism.
What if the worker crashes while its dispatch is still in flight?

A crash should not be assumed to settle the reservation merely because the worker becomes unreachable. The model-checking question is whether the specified guards keep that credit out of a conflicting reassignment until its outstanding use has been safely accounted for. The plan does not provide a crash-recovery procedure.
How should the model check treat a dispatch that was sent before expiry but arrives after reclamation?

It should be able to distinguish sending the dispatch from its possible acceptance. Otherwise it could miss a credit that appears eligible for reclamation while an old in-flight dispatch can still use it. The guard and worker-acceptance rules would have to agree at that boundary; the plan does not yet state exactly how such a dispatch is handled.
What is the core safety question for partitioned-worker reclamation?

Can any permitted execution make a credit spendable through the partitioned worker’s old slice or an outstanding reservation while also making that same credit spendable after reclamation? The model check is intended to examine that question under the guards to be specified. It does not come with a pass result.
Should the check look only at who is recorded as owning the slice?

That would leave out outstanding reservations and worker acceptance. A recorded ownership change may not prevent an old in-flight dispatch from consuming a credit. The reclamation check needs enough accounting to examine both the assigned slice and any unsettled claims on its credits.
Do quorum-certified slices eliminate the need for those guards?

No. Certification addresses the authority of an assignment; it does not automatically settle dispatches already using that assignment or define when the old authority expires. The slice-expiry and reservation-settlement guards are the planned conditions for deciding what may be reclaimed from a partitioned worker.
Can a worker in a partition keep spending its preassigned credits while the check is running?

The proposed partition rule permits only spending within credits preassigned to that worker. The model must not treat the partition itself as creating more credits. It also must not reclaim a credit as spendable elsewhere while the old worker or an outstanding dispatch remains authorized to use that same credit.
Does model-checking reclamation automatically establish that credits will eventually be reclaimed?

No. A check that rules out overlap is a safety check. An eventual-reclamation claim would need its own stated progress condition and assumptions about what can proceed during a partition. This plan calls for model-checking partitioned-worker reclamation, but gives neither a progress bound nor a reported result.
Why put the dispatch-isolation benchmark after the model check?

That is the order stated in the plan: define the reclaim rules and examine them under partitioned-worker behavior before evaluating dispatch isolation. It keeps the quota-reclamation question and the performance measurement distinct. The ordering does not imply that a successful model check, if obtained, would predict the benchmark’s latency result.
What does the later benchmark need to measure?

It needs to assess dispatch isolation on healthy workers. For the scheduler’s performance requirement, the relevant comparison is unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency against their workload-matched isolated baselines, with a target of no more than 2×. This plan does not name a benchmark configuration or report a measured latency.
Would a good healthy-worker p99 result validate slice reclamation too?

No. Latency does not establish that quota ownership remains unique or that outstanding reservations were settled before credits were reclaimed. Likewise, a model-checking result about reclamation would not measure unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency. The plan calls for both evaluations because they address different requirements.
Can I already specify a numerical reclaim time or a p99 measurement in the plan?

Neither is supplied here. The plan names slice-expiry and reservation-settlement guards, a model check for partitioned-worker reclamation, and a later healthy-worker isolation benchmark. It does not give a slice lifetime, a time-to-reclaim bound, or a benchmark result; adding those as established figures would go beyond the plan.
What should I say if someone asks whether the guards have been verified?

Say that specifying the guards and model-checking reclamation are planned activities. No completed specification or model-checking outcome is stated in this step. The benchmark is also planned for afterward, so there is no new healthy-worker latency result to quote.
Can you give me a concise formulation of the sequence?

“Specify slice-expiry and reservation-settlement guards; model-check reclamation from partitioned workers for overlap with outstanding reservations; then benchmark dispatch isolation on healthy workers.” That preserves the order and the distinct safety and performance questions without claiming either has already been answered.

Let’s extend the IsolateMix-24 replay bundle with partitioned quorum-certified slices and expiry-fenced reservations, then check duplicate ownership and healthy-worker p99 dispatch latency. What is this activity examining?

It puts the proposed per-worker credit slices and reservation rules into a replay that also examines dispatch performance. The replay must distinguish credits assigned to one worker from credits assigned to another, and distinguish an existing certified assignment from a proposed reassignment. Otherwise it could not meaningfully check whether ownership duplicates during a partition. The activity does not specify the certificate format, slice sizes, or the procedure for issuing them.
Does a partitioned worker get a new quota slice simply because it cannot reach the quorum?

No. The proposed partition rule is that a worker spends only credits preassigned to it. Loss of connectivity does not create credits or enlarge a certified slice. The replay should retain that distinction when examining what the partitioned worker can do.
And what do expiry-fenced reservations add to the scenario?

They make outstanding uses of credits relevant to the handoff. A credit reserved for a dispatch should not be treated as freely available elsewhere while the old dispatch can still use it. Is expiry of a worker’s slice necessarily the same as expiry of a reservation within it?

What should the duplicate-ownership check ask at a partition boundary?

It should ask whether a credit remains owned under a partitioned worker’s certified slice while also being assigned elsewhere. If both sides of a partition have certificates, is that automatically a duplicate-owner finding?

Could an ownership check ignore reservations because reservations are about spending?

That would risk overlooking the handoff boundary the activity is meant to exercise. Does ‘check duplicate ownership’ mean this is already a completed model-checking run?

What does the IsolateMix-24 replay bundle contribute here?

It is the replay artifact being extended, rather than an entirely new named test. Does this activity prescribe how many workers or tenants the partition separates?

If a worker has an outstanding reservation when it becomes partitioned, can the replay assume that credit has been reclaimed?

Would worker silence be sufficient evidence that its slice can be reassigned?

What if a dispatch using an old reservation arrives after another worker receives a slice?

That is a relevant boundary to represent when examining overlapping claims. The check should not assume an in-flight dispatch vanished merely because a new slice was certified. Whether the old dispatch can still be accepted, and whether its reserved credit was included in the new assignment, determine whether the handoff is safe. No trace or outcome for that case is reported here.
Does the replay change the rule that a partitioned worker spends only preassigned credits?

No change to that rule is stated. The replay extension is meant to exercise partitioned workers with quorum-certified slices and expiry-fenced reservations. It should not interpret a partition, or a worker’s local need for work, as authority to exceed its preassigned credits.
Turning to performance, whose p99 are we checking?

The activity names healthy-worker p99. In the scheduler’s isolation requirement, the relevant measure is unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers against their workload-matched isolated baseline. The activity gives no measured p99 or revised numerical benchmark threshold.
Could a good overall throughput figure replace the healthy-worker p99 check?

Does ‘healthy worker’ mean the replay cannot contain crashes or partitions?

If duplicate ownership is absent, can we skip measuring p99?

And if healthy-worker p99 is acceptable, can we infer the slices never overlap?

Does this activity tell us whether the dedicated dispatch cores or eight-event drain limits need to change?

No change to either is specified. Could I claim the replay establishes that reservations eventually expire and every slice is reclaimed?

Not from the checks named here. Expiry-fenced reservations are included, but the stated checks are duplicate ownership and healthy-worker p99. The activity does not report an eventual-reclamation property, a time-to-reclaim bound, or an outcome under loss of quorum.

That is the reported ownership observation for the 10,000 partitioned slice migrations: no overlap was found. It should remain tied to those migrations rather than becoming a claim about every possible slice assignment or failure sequence.
Is the 100/100 figure another way of saying no ownership overlap?

No. They are separate observations. “No overlapping ownership” addresses conflicting ownership claims; “peak credits 100/100” reports that the recorded credit count reached no more than 100 against 100. Keeping both statements preserves what was actually reported without treating one as a substitute for the other.
Can I say all 100 credits were spent on every migration?

No. A peak of 100/100 does not say that 100 credits were spent, nor that the peak occurred in every migration. It reports the maximum credit count against the 100-credit allocation across the stated tests; no breakdown of that peak is provided.
Does the result report whether every partitioned worker stayed within its own certified slice?

It does not give a separate per-worker spending figure. No overlapping ownership and a 100/100 peak are relevant to the proposal that partitioned workers spend only preassigned credits, but they should not be relabeled as a reported measurement of each worker’s spending against its individual slice.
Can I describe the 10,000 as model-checked states?
No. The number is 10,000 partitioned slice migrations in IsolateMix-24. It is not a count of model states, workers, dispatches, or distinct partition topologies.
Does ‘partitioned slice migrations’ tell us how long the partitions lasted?

No. The result identifies migrations under partitions but gives no partition duration, connectivity pattern, or quorum-availability history. Those details should not be inferred from the migration count.
What exactly is the 4.2 ms measurement?
It is the reported p99 *dispatch latency* for unaffected tenants on healthy workers in IsolateMix-24. It is not average dispatch latency, execution time, or a p99 for unhealthy workers.
Can you verify the 1.75× ratio?
Yes. For this workload-matched comparison, the isolated p99 is 2.4 ms; 4.2 ms divided by 2.4 ms is 1.75. The 1.75× figure is a ratio, while 4.2 ms is the measured dispatch latency.
How does 4.2 ms compare with the 2× threshold?

Twice the matched isolated p99 of 2.4 ms is 4.8 ms. The measured 4.2 ms is 0.6 ms below that threshold, and its 1.75× ratio is below 2×. That comparison holds for the unaffected healthy-worker p99 reported in IsolateMix-24.
Does 4.2 ms mean no dispatch took longer than 4.2 ms?
No. A p99 is not a maximum for individual dispatches. The finding does not give the longest dispatch latency or a complete latency distribution.
Do we know that each unaffected tenant individually had a p99 of exactly 4.2 ms?
No tenant-by-tenant breakdown is stated. Report the 4.2 ms unaffected healthy-worker p99 in its given scope; do not assign that exact value to every unaffected tenant separately.
Does ‘1.75× isolated’ imply there was no cross-tenant interference?

No. It says the reported p99 was 1.75 times the isolated comparison, so the measured latency was above isolation. The narrower conclusion is that it stayed within the stated 2× threshold in IsolateMix-24.
Can I attribute the 4.2 ms entirely to dedicated dispatch cores?

The result does not isolate a single component’s contribution. IsolateMix-24 examined the proposed arrangement with partitioned quorum-certified slices and expiry-fenced reservations in the replay bundle. The measured p99 describes that tested arrangement; it does not quantify how much of the result came from dedicated dispatch cores or any other component.
Do these observations tell us exactly when an outstanding reservation was settled?
No. They report ownership overlap, peak credits, and p99 dispatch latency. They do not give a reservation-settlement trace or a time-to-reclaim bound for any slice.
Can I conclude that an unavailable quorum would never strand credits?

No. The result provides no reassignment-time observation or finding about what happens when quorum is unavailable. Its reported scope is the 10,000 partitioned slice migrations and their ownership, credit-peak, and latency observations.
Would the p99 result alone establish quota safety?

No. Dispatch latency and quota ownership measure different properties. This finding separately reports no overlapping ownership and a 100/100 peak credit count; those are the observations relevant to the quota side. The 4.2 ms p99 addresses performance isolation.
And would no overlapping ownership alone establish the healthy-worker latency target?
No. Ownership safety does not measure dispatch delay. Here, the separate 4.2 ms p99 measurement—1.75× the matched isolated value—is what supports the latency comparison within this benchmark.
Can I say the proposal is proven safe and fast for every adversarial workload and network partition?

That would exceed the evidence. The reported results support the proposed approach in IsolateMix-24 across 10,000 partitioned slice migrations, with the stated ownership, credit, and latency observations. They do not enumerate every adversarial workload, partition topology, or possible execution.
What is a concise version that keeps all three numbers and the main qualifiers?

“In IsolateMix-24, 10,000 partitioned slice migrations showed no overlapping ownership and peak credits of 100/100; unaffected tenants’ healthy-worker p99 dispatch latency was 4.2 ms (1.75× isolated, within the 2× target).”

I want to model-check slice reclamation under asymmetric partitions, delayed acknowledgments, and ±2-second clock skew. The check should assert that credits remain reserved until worker-enforced expiry. What is the central question?

Whether the reclamation rules ever make a reserved credit available under a new slice before worker-enforced expiry has ended its old use. The model check should examine that boundary when communication is asymmetric, acknowledgments are delayed, and clocks differ within the stated ±2-second skew. This describes the property to check, not a result.
Why does the assertion refer to worker-enforced expiry rather than a scheduler deciding that enough time has passed?

The worker is where an outstanding dispatch could still be accepted. A scheduler’s view of the clock does not, by itself, establish that the worker has stopped accepting use of the reserved credit. The assertion makes release contingent on expiry being enforced at that boundary, rather than merely inferred elsewhere.
Does expiry of a quota slice automatically end every reservation within that slice?

The activity does not equate the two. Slice expiry concerns the assignment being reclaimed; worker-enforced expiry is the stated boundary for credits that remain reserved. The check should not treat the end of a slice assignment as permission to release an outstanding reservation before the worker-enforced condition holds.
What is asymmetric about the partitions we need to model?

Participants must not be assumed to have identical connectivity or to learn of reclamation at the same time. A worker might still be reachable along a path that another participant cannot use. The activity calls for asymmetric partitions but does not specify a particular topology, so the check needs to represent unequal views without assuming one named connectivity pattern.
If the old worker cannot acknowledge reclamation, can its silence count as expiry?

No. A delayed or missing acknowledgment is not worker-enforced expiry. Under the stated assertion, the credit remains reserved until that expiry condition is met, regardless of whether the acknowledgment is promptly available. The model should not turn a communication delay into permission to reclaim a reserved credit.
Could an acknowledgment arrive after a new slice has been certified?

That is an ordering a model check can examine without presuming it is safe or unsafe. The essential test is whether a delayed acknowledgment can cause the accounting to release or reassign a credit that must still remain reserved until worker-enforced expiry. This activity does not prescribe how certificates or acknowledgments are represented.
Why include clock skew of ±2 seconds?

It makes timing uncertainty part of the reclamation check. Participants’ views of an expiry boundary may differ within the specified ±2-second skew, so the assertion must not depend on every participant observing expiry simultaneously. The activity does not state an expiry duration or an exact formula for applying the skew allowance.
Can I turn ±2-second skew into a fixed time after which all reserved credits transfer?

No. Skew is a bound on clock variation in the check, not a complete reclaim schedule. Worker-enforced expiry must still be defined and applied; the activity gives no universal transfer time or duration for which credits remain reserved.
What should the model record about a credit before attempting reclamation?

It needs enough state to distinguish a credit still reserved for an outstanding use from one eligible to be reclaimed, and enough worker behavior to determine whether expiry has been enforced. The activity specifies the assertion but does not provide the state variables or accounting formula, so those are modeling requirements rather than a supplied implementation.
Is it sufficient to check only that the new worker has a quorum-certified slice?

No. Certification of a new assignment does not resolve a credit’s old reservation. For this activity, the important question is whether the credit remains reserved until worker-enforced expiry even as reclamation and certification proceed under a partition. A valid new slice cannot make an outstanding old use disappear by itself.
If a reserved credit appears in a new slice before worker-enforced expiry, what would that mean for the check?

It would challenge the stated assertion if the credit had thereby become available while it was still required to remain reserved. The model must distinguish merely proposing a reclamation from actually releasing or reassigning a reserved credit. That is an interpretation of a possible counterexample, not an observed finding.
Could we model a partition by freezing every participant until connectivity returns?

That would miss the point of examining reclamation under asymmetric partitions. Some participants may still act or exchange messages while others cannot. The check should not assume that disconnection stops all old uses or that every participant resumes with a common view at once. No particular pattern of continued activity is specified here.
Do delayed acknowledgments necessarily indicate that the worker has crashed?
No. The activity names delayed acknowledgments, not their cause. They should be represented as delayed information without inferring a crash, completion, or enforced expiry from the delay alone.
Is this asserting that the entire slice must remain reserved until expiry?

The assertion is about credits that remain reserved. It should not silently classify every credit in a slice as an outstanding reservation. The model must make clear which credits are reserved and ensure that reclamation does not release those credits before worker-enforced expiry.
Could the check pass by never reclaiming any slice at all?

A model that never reclaims credits might satisfy a narrow ‘do not release before expiry’ safety assertion while leaving the reclamation question unresolved. The activity is to model-check slice reclamation as well as assert the reservation boundary. A separate progress property would be needed to claim that eligible credits are eventually reclaimed; no such outcome or bound is stated here.
Does this activity establish a maximum time for reclaiming credits from a partitioned worker?

No. It supplies ±2-second skew as a checking condition but no numerical slice lifetime, execution-expiry duration, or time-to-reclaim target. It asks whether reclamation preserves reservations until worker-enforced expiry, not whether reclamation completes by a stated deadline.
Does it check unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency too?

No. This activity concerns slice reclamation and reserved-credit safety under asymmetric partitions, delayed acknowledgments, and ±2-second skew. It does not call for a healthy-worker p99 benchmark or report a latency measurement. Credit safety and dispatch isolation remain separate questions.
Would the absence of an assertion violation prove every partitioned worker stays within its assigned quota?

Not from this assertion alone. Keeping credits reserved until worker-enforced expiry is relevant to preventing premature reuse during reclamation. A claim about every worker’s individual spending limit would require that limit to be represented and checked as well. This activity reports no model-checking outcome in any case.
How do I state the work without implying the guards have passed?

“Model-check slice reclamation under asymmetric partitions, delayed acknowledgments, and ±2-second clock skew, asserting that reserved credits remain reserved until worker-enforced expiry.” That gives the conditions and the safety property without claiming a completed result.

The slice-reclamation model found a 14-step trace: a slice was reclaimed at 30 seconds while an outstanding reservation did not expire until 40 seconds, and credit use reached 101/100. What does that establish?

It is a counterexample to safe reclamation in the modeled behavior. Reclaiming at 30 seconds made credits available while a reservation remained outstanding until 40 seconds; the trace reached 101 credits against an allocation of 100. The quorum-certified slice and expiry-fenced reservation arrangement, as represented in this trace, did not prevent overlapping credit use.
Is the problem simply that 30 is less than 40?

That ordering exposes the gap: slice reclamation occurred before the reservation’s expiry. The decisive observation is that the gap permitted credit use to reach 101/100. The two times alone would not tell us how many credits were used; the trace supplies that result.
Does this say the reservation actually remained spendable after the slice was reclaimed?

The trace shows reclamation overlapping a reservation that expired at 40 seconds and an ensuing 101/100-credit state. That establishes that the modeled rules allowed conflicting use across the boundary. It does not provide a detailed account of which worker accepted which dispatch.
Can I call the difference a ten-second overspend?

No. Reclamation at 30 seconds and reservation expiry at 40 seconds are ten seconds apart, but the evidence does not say the excess credit was spent for that entire interval. The reported overspend is one credit beyond 100 in a 14-step trace, not a ten-second duration of excess spending.
What does the 14-step figure measure?

It is the length of the model’s counterexample trace in steps. It is not 14 seconds, 14 migrations, or a count of dispatches. The stated times in that trace are the reclaim at 30 seconds and reservation expiry at 40 seconds.
Does 101/100 refer to two owners, or to credits?

To credits: the trace reached 101 against a 100-credit allocation. That is direct evidence of exceeding the credit bound. The result does not separately report a count of duplicate owners, so it is more precise to describe the observed failure as overlapping reservation and reclamation leading to 101/100 credits.
Could both the old and new workers have stayed within their own locally recorded slices?

The result does not give per-worker balances, so it cannot answer that. It does show why local limits alone would be an incomplete account of this trace: the modeled reclamation overlapped an outstanding reservation, and the total reached 101/100. We should not invent which participant spent the excess credit.
Does quorum certification make reclaiming at 30 seconds safe despite the reservation expiring at 40?

Not in this modeled trace. Certification of a reclaimed slice did not prevent the reported overlap with the outstanding reservation or the 101/100 result. The counterexample concerns the interaction between reclamation and reservation expiry; it does not tell us that quorum certification was absent or identify an internal certificate defect.
Did the worker fail to enforce the 40-second expiry?

That is not established. The reported reservation expiry is at 40 seconds, and reclamation happened earlier, at 30 seconds. The trace does not say that the worker accepted a dispatch after 40 seconds or failed to enforce expiry then. The demonstrated gap is making credit available through reclamation while its reservation had not yet expired.
Can we blame the ±2-second clock skew for the ten-second difference?

No. The model-checking activity included ±2-second skew, but the reported trace does not attribute the 30-versus-40-second overlap to skew or give the clocks’ values. The 101/100 outcome should not be assigned a more specific cause than the evidence provides.
What about asymmetric partitions and delayed acknowledgments—do we know their precise role in this trace?

The check examined slice reclamation under those conditions, but the stated finding does not give the partition topology, acknowledgment ordering, or a step-by-step explanation of their contribution. We can identify the trace as a result of that model check without reconstructing unreported events.
Does this mean every slice reclamation at 30 seconds will overspend?

No. It means at least one permitted 14-step execution in the slice-reclamation model reaches 101/100 when reclamation at 30 seconds overlaps a reservation expiring at 40 seconds. A single counterexample defeats an unconditional safety claim for the modeled rules, but it does not establish that every reclamation has the same outcome.
Is it enough to say the reservation should be held until 40 seconds?

The trace shows that reclaiming the credit while its reservation remained outstanding was unsafe. It does not, by itself, establish a complete alternative release rule: the model would still need to say what worker-enforced expiry means and when a formerly reserved credit may safely become available. The reported finding is a failure trace, not a verified repair.
Could we simply change slice reclaim time from 30 to 40 seconds and declare the problem solved?

The counterexample does not justify that conclusion. Aligning two timestamps might address this particular ordering, but safety also depends on how expiry is enforced and whether other outstanding reservations or delayed dispatches remain spendable. No modified rule or check of it is reported here.
Does this result imply the dedicated dispatch cores caused an overspend?

No. Dedicated dispatch cores concern dispatch processing capacity. The reported failure is the overlap between slice reclamation and an outstanding reservation, with credits reaching 101/100. The trace supplies no causal finding about the cores or a dispatch-latency measurement.
Can I say the slice-and-reservation proposal is safe if the p99 dispatch latency is good?

No. A p99 latency result would not erase the 101/100 counterexample. This trace challenges quota safety in the modeled slice-reclamation behavior; it says nothing about unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers. The two requirements must be assessed separately.
Does the trace tell us how long any credits were stranded?

No. It reports premature overlap and excess credits, not a time-to-reclaim or stranding result. The 30-second reclaim and 40-second reservation expiry identify the timing of this safety counterexample, not a bound on how long credits remain unavailable in other executions.
How narrowly should I characterize the finding against the proposed per-worker slices?

Say that the slice-reclamation model permits a 14-step counterexample in which reclamation at 30 seconds overlaps a reservation expiring at 40 seconds and reaches 101/100 credits. That refutes the sufficiency of the modeled reclamation arrangement for preventing overlap in that execution. It does not identify a complete fix or establish a performance result.
Give me a concise sentence for the result.
“The slice-reclamation model found a 14-step counterexample: reclaiming at 30 seconds overlapped a reservation expiring at 40 seconds, allowing credits to reach 101/100.”

I’ve decided to defer quorum-certified slices despite the 4.2 ms p99 dispatch latency. Reclamation at 30 seconds overlaps reservations lasting until 40 seconds and exceeds the 100-credit cap. How should I state the decision?

“Defer quorum-certified slices despite the 4.2 ms p99: reclaiming a slice at 30 seconds can overlap reservations that remain outstanding until 40 seconds, exceeding the 100-credit cap.” That states both the favorable latency observation and the quota-safety reason for deferral, without implying that the overlap has been resolved.
Why doesn’t the 4.2 ms p99 outweigh the credit issue?

The requirements are independent. The 4.2 ms p99 concerns dispatch latency; it cannot authorize spending beyond a 100-credit cap. Deferring the slices reflects the stated decision not to accept that quota-safety gap on the strength of the latency observation.
Is the 4.2 ms figure a credit-reclamation time?

No. It is a p99 dispatch-latency figure, measured in milliseconds. The reclamation and reservation times in the decision are 30 seconds and 40 seconds. Mixing those units would obscure why the credit cap is at issue.
What exactly overlaps at 30 and 40 seconds?

The slice is reclaimed at 30 seconds while its outstanding reservations continue until 40 seconds. For that interval, reclamation can make credits available under a new claim before the old reservations have ended. The stated consequence is an exceedance of the 100-credit cap; the decision does not specify how long the excess spending lasts.
Does that mean the reclamation happens repeatedly every 30 seconds?
No. “Reclamation at 30 seconds” identifies the reclaim point in the stated case. It is not a claim about a recurring 30-second schedule or every slice’s lifetime.
Is the difference between 30 and 40 seconds a ten-second latency penalty?

No. The times are ten seconds apart, but they concern reclamation and reservation expiry, not dispatch latency. Nor does their difference establish that credits were over the cap for exactly ten seconds.
Why isn’t a quorum certificate enough to make the reclaimed slice safe?

Certification of a new assignment does not, by itself, settle reservations that remain outstanding under the old assignment. The decision identifies precisely that mismatch: reclamation at 30 seconds overlaps reservations lasting until 40 seconds, with credit use exceeding the 100-credit cap. The certificate cannot be treated as permission for the same credits to support both claims.
Can I say all quorum-certified slices are inherently unsafe?

No. The decision is to defer them because of the stated 30-second reclamation and 40-second reservation overlap. It does not establish that every possible slice protocol, timing rule, or configuration has the same defect.
Does ‘defer’ mean permanently reject the idea?
No. Deferral means the decision is not to adopt quorum-certified slices at this point. It does not state a permanent rejection, a replacement design, or a completed remedy.
Could I describe the 4.2 ms as an unaffected-tenant healthy-worker p99?

Yes; that identifies the dispatch-latency measurement being referenced. Keep it distinct from the 100-credit cap. The decision mentions the p99 despite choosing to defer the slices because the reclamation overlap presents a separate quota problem.
Does the decision say exactly how far above 100 credits the system went?
No. It says the 100-credit cap was exceeded. A precise peak beyond that cap is not part of this decision’s wording, so a concise statement of the decision need not supply one.
Should I present the overlap as a mere possibility that we have not observed?
No. The decision states the overlap and cap exceedance as its reason for deferral. At the same time, it should not be broadened into a claim that every partitioned reclamation exceeds the cap.
If the slice is reclaimed at 30 seconds, can I simply assume all its reservations are finished then?
No. The stated reservations last until 40 seconds. Treating them as finished at 30 seconds would erase the very overlap on which the decision is based.
Would changing reclamation from 30 seconds to 40 seconds establish a safe protocol?

That is not established by this decision. The 30-versus-40-second mismatch explains the identified cap exceedance, but the decision neither specifies a revised reclaim guard nor reports that any revised rule has been checked. It says to defer quorum-certified slices, not that a particular timing adjustment has solved the problem.
Is this a decision about whether the dispatch-core arrangement works?

No. The decision specifically defers quorum-certified slices and gives the reservation overlap and 100-credit-cap exceedance as the reason, despite the 4.2 ms p99. It does not make a new decision about dispatch cores or assign them responsibility for the credit overlap.
Can we say the 4.2 ms observation establishes quota safety in the conditions where it was measured?

No. A p99 dispatch-latency measurement does not measure whether credits are reclaimed safely. The decision explicitly keeps those concerns apart: it cites the 4.2 ms p99 but defers the slices because the 30-second reclaim conflicts with reservations lasting until 40 seconds and exceeds the 100-credit cap.
What is the central boundary a future slice-reclamation rule would have to respect?

It would have to avoid making credits spendable through reclamation while outstanding reservations can still use them. That is the conceptual boundary illustrated by the 30-second and 40-second overlap. The decision does not select or validate a future rule for enforcing it.
How narrowly should I word the reason for deferral?

Tie it to the stated case: reclamation at 30 seconds overlaps reservations lasting until 40 seconds, and the resulting credit use exceeds the 100-credit cap. Avoid turning that into an unreported claim about every partition, every reservation, or an exact duration of overspending.
Give me one short sentence that keeps the favorable p99 and the safety decision together.
“Defer quorum-certified slices despite 4.2 ms p99 dispatch latency: 30-second reclamation overlaps 40-second reservations and exceeds the 100-credit cap.”

I propose reclaiming quorum-certified slices only after both the slice and all outstanding reservations have expired, plus a clock-skew allowance. I would retain dedicated dispatch cores and eight-event drains. How do these pieces fit together?

The reclaim rule concerns quota safety: credits in a slice must not be reassigned while either the slice’s authority or an outstanding reservation on those credits can still be used. The clock-skew allowance is part of the proposed timing boundary. Dedicated dispatch cores and eight-event drains remain the performance-isolation components. This is a proposal, not a finding that the revised reclaim rule or the combined design has passed a check.
Is it enough for the slice itself to expire?

No. The proposed condition requires both the slice’s expiry and the expiries of its outstanding reservations, plus skew, before reclamation. Slice expiry alone must not be treated as proof that a dispatch holding a reservation can no longer use its credits.
If one outstanding reservation expires later than the others, which expiry matters?

That later outstanding reservation still prevents reclamation under the proposed rule. The condition is not satisfied until the slice and all outstanding reservations have expired, with the skew allowance accounted for. The proposal does not specify the individual expiry times or a precise timestamp calculation.
Does ‘plus skew’ mean adding a fixed number of seconds to every reservation?

It means the reclaim boundary must include an allowance for clock skew. This proposal does not give a numerical skew bound or define exactly how the allowance is calculated. I would not turn it into a particular number of seconds or an exact reclaim deadline without those details.
Could a partitioned worker continue using its certified slice while that slice remains valid?

The proposed partition rule permits a worker to spend only credits preassigned to it. Reclamation must not make those credits spendable elsewhere while the worker can still use them under its slice or through outstanding reservations. A partition does not enlarge the worker’s assignment or make its credits automatically reclaimable.
Why does quorum certification not settle the reservation question on its own?

Certification identifies the authority for a slice; it does not establish that every dispatch already holding a reservation has expired. The proposed reclaim condition therefore accounts for the slice and its outstanding reservations separately. A new assignment must not rely on the certificate alone to erase an old spendable claim.
Could we reclaim the slice when its worker stops answering, provided a quorum approves?

Not under this proposal solely on those grounds. Nonresponse does not establish expiry of the slice or of all outstanding reservations. Quorum certification does not replace the stated expiry-plus-skew conditions for reclaiming credits.
Does waiting for all reservations mean the whole slice is necessarily unavailable for new work until then?

The proposal says to reclaim quorum-certified slices only after the slice and outstanding reservations expire plus skew. It does not specify partial reclamation or how other credits are used while reclamation is pending. We should not infer a more detailed rule about partial transfers or continued dispatch from this statement.
How should I distinguish slice expiry from reservation expiry in the design description?

Slice expiry is the boundary on the worker’s assignment of quota credits. An outstanding reservation is a claim associated with work that may still use some of those credits. The proposed reclaim rule requires both kinds of claim to reach their expiry boundaries before the slice is reclaimed; one boundary cannot silently substitute for the other.
If a reservation’s timestamp has passed on one machine, can reclamation proceed immediately?

The proposal does not authorize reclamation from one machine’s apparent expiry alone. It expressly adds skew to the slice and outstanding-reservation expiry conditions. A concrete protocol would need to define when those conditions can safely be regarded as satisfied and what workers may still accept; those details are not specified here.
Does this proposal itself guarantee an old in-flight dispatch will be rejected after reclamation?

No. Waiting for the stated expiry boundaries is the proposed reclaim guard, but the statement does not define a complete worker-admission or fencing protocol for delayed messages. Preventing overlapping credit use still depends on those expiry boundaries being effective wherever an old dispatch could be accepted. That outcome has not been demonstrated by the proposal alone.
Is there a time-to-reclaim guarantee here?

No numerical bound is given. Reclamation is conditioned on the slice and every outstanding reservation expiring plus skew; the proposal supplies neither those expiry durations nor a guaranteed time for carrying out reclamation afterward. It should not be presented as a specific stranding bound.
What if an outstanding reservation cannot yet be confirmed as expired?

Then the stated reclaim condition has not been established for that reservation. The proposal does not allow uncertainty to be treated as expiry. It also does not provide an alternative settlement or recovery rule for that case.
Why retain dedicated dispatch cores in a proposal about quota-slice reclamation?

They address a different requirement. Slice and reservation expiry constrain when quota may move; dedicated dispatch cores are intended to protect dispatch processing from competing work. Keeping the cores in the proposed combination does not make reclamation safer by itself, and safe reclamation alone does not establish low dispatch latency.
And what do the eight-event drains contribute?

They retain a limit on the amount of completion work handled in a drain. Eight is an event count, not a credit count or a millisecond limit. The proposal does not say that an event drain itself releases a reservation or grants a worker credits.
Are the eight-event drains a way to make the outstanding reservations expire faster?

No such connection is stated. Drain limits organize processing; the proposed reclaim guard still waits for the slice and outstanding reservation expiries plus skew. Processing completion events and establishing an expiry boundary are not interchangeable simply because both may matter during migration.
Could a worker’s dedicated dispatch core let it spend credits after its slice expires?

No. A dedicated core is processing capacity, not quota authority. The worker remains limited to credits validly assigned to it. The proposed expiry guard must not be bypassed because dispatch capacity is available.
Does the proposal change the number of credits assigned to any worker?

No slice size or credit amount is specified. It changes the proposed condition for reclaiming quorum-certified slices while retaining dedicated dispatch cores and eight-event drains. It does not state a new quota allocation.
If the slice has expired but an old reservation has not, what is the crucial safety point?

The reservation still matters. Under the proposal, the slice is not reclaimable merely because its own expiry has passed: an outstanding reservation that has not expired must remain accounted for so its credit is not made spendable through a new assignment as well.
And if all reservations have expired but the slice itself has not?

The other condition still blocks reclamation. The proposed rule requires slice expiry as well as expiry of all outstanding reservations, plus skew. It is an AND condition, not permission to reclaim whenever either side expires first.
Does the proposal establish that unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency meets the 2× target?

No. Retaining dedicated dispatch cores and eight-event drains keeps performance-isolation mechanisms in the design, but this proposal reports no latency measurement. The target remains unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency on healthy workers within 2× their workload-matched isolated baseline.
Would a good p99 measurement establish that the revised reclaim boundary is safe?

No. Dispatch latency and quota ownership are distinct. A latency result could assess the retained processing arrangement, but the proposed reclaim guard would still need evaluation for overlapping authority and outstanding reservations during migration or partitions.
Could I describe the proposal as a verified repair for partitioned-worker reclamation?

No. It proposes a more restrictive reclaim condition: wait for slice expiry and all outstanding reservation expiries plus skew. It does not include a completed specification, model-checking result, or observed credit bound for that condition.
How can I summarize the design choice without implying an outcome?

“Propose reclaiming quorum-certified slices only after both the slice and all outstanding reservations expire, with a clock-skew allowance, while retaining dedicated dispatch cores and eight-event drains.” That preserves the quota-safety condition and the performance components without claiming they have been validated together.

Here is my hypothesis for reclaiming a quorum-certified slice from a partitioned worker: wait until max(slice expiry, reservation expiries) plus a 4-second clock-skew margin. I predict that this prevents duplicate ownership while retaining unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency at ≤4.8 ms. Is that precise?

It states two testable predictions, but they remain hypotheses. For reclamation, take the later of the slice’s expiry and the expiries of its outstanding reservations, then wait an additional 4 seconds before reclaiming the slice. The safety prediction is that this prevents duplicate ownership. The separate performance prediction is that unaffected tenants’ p99 dispatch latency remains ≤4.8 ms in the healthy-worker, workload-matched isolation comparison. The timing rule alone does not establish either outcome.
Does “max” mean I can use whichever expiry I happen to observe first?

No. It means the latest relevant expiry governs: the slice expiry or the expiry of any outstanding reservation, whichever is later. Reclaiming after the first expiry would not express the proposed rule.
Suppose the slice expires before one of its reservations. What does the hypothesis require?
Reclamation waits for that later reservation expiry and then the additional 4-second skew margin. The slice’s earlier expiry does not make an outstanding reservation irrelevant.
What if every reservation expires first but the slice remains valid?

Then the slice expiry is the maximum, and the proposed reclaim point is after that expiry plus the 4-second margin. Both categories of expiry matter; satisfying only the reservation side is insufficient.
Am I adding four seconds to each expiry before taking the maximum?

The hypothesis is most directly expressed as max(slice expiry, reservation expiries) plus a 4-second skew margin. Because the same margin applies to the governing latest expiry, the key requirement is that reclamation does not precede that latest expiry plus 4 seconds. This wording does not specify how timestamps are represented or checked.
Is the 4-second margin a new lease duration?
No. It is a clock-skew margin added after the governing expiry, not the duration of a slice or an outstanding reservation. The hypothesis does not state either of those durations.
Does that margin establish that every worker has learned about the reclamation?

No. A timing margin is not, by itself, a communication guarantee. To support the no-duplicate-ownership prediction, the expiry and any enforcement of old claims must be defined so that the old slice or reservation cannot remain spendable when the credits are made available under another owner. The hypothesis proposes the waiting boundary but does not spell out a complete worker-admission protocol.
Why does the rule mention reservation expiries as well as slice expiry if ownership concerns the slice?

An outstanding reservation may still claim credits from that slice for a dispatch.
